lessons.title: Series and DataFrame
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 1: Series and DataFrame

theory.contentHtml:
You have the average scores of four students and you want to keep each name attached to its number. In plain Python you have to choose: a dict, or two parallel lists plus your own memory that the third element of one list matches the third element of the other. pandas ships a type built for exactly this:

import pandas as pd

scores = pd.Series([8.5, 7.0, 9.0, 6.5], index=["An", "Binh", "Chi", "Dung"])
print(scores)
An      8.5
Binh    7.0
Chi     9.0
Dung    6.5
dtype: float64

A Series is a sequence of values paired with a sequence of labels, and that sequence of labels is called the index. The left column of the printout is the index, the right column is the values. Because of that, every number always knows who it belongs to, no matter what position it currently sits in.

Several Series on one index make a table

The score is one piece of information, the number of absences is another, and both talk about those same four people. Line the two Series up on the same index:

import pandas as pd

scores = pd.Series([8.5, 7.0, 9.0, 6.5], index=["An", "Binh", "Chi", "Dung"])
absences = pd.Series([0, 2, 1, 3], index=["An", "Binh", "Chi", "Dung"])
students = pd.DataFrame({"score": scores, "absence": absences})
print(students)
      score  absence
An      8.5        0
Binh    7.0        2
Chi     9.0        1
Dung    6.5        3

A DataFrame is several Series sharing one index. Each column keeps its own data type - score is floating point, absence is integer - but they share exactly the same four row labels, so reading across one row gives you one person's whole record.

Pulling out a column gives you a Series again

import pandas as pd

students = pd.DataFrame(
    {"score": [8.5, 7.0, 9.0, 6.5], "absence": [0, 2, 1, 3]},
    index=["An", "Binh", "Chi", "Dung"],
)
one_column = students["score"]
print(type(one_column).__name__)
print(one_column.index.tolist())
print(students.index.tolist())
Series
['An', 'Binh', 'Chi', 'Dung']
['An', 'Binh', 'Chi', 'Dung']

The column you take out carries the table's index with it instead of being a loose list. That is why you can put it back into another table, or compare it against another column, without rows drifting out of alignment.

lessons.title: Building a DataFrame from Python data
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 2: Building a DataFrame from Python data

theory.contentHtml:
Real data rarely arrives as Series. Usually what you are holding is a dict of lists - each key is a column name, each list holds that column's values from top to bottom. Hand that dict straight to pd.DataFrame:

import pandas as pd

products = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Keyboard", "Mouse", "Monitor"],
    "price": [450000, 180000, 2500000],
})
print(products)
       name    price
0  Keyboard   450000
1     Mouse   180000
2   Monitor  2500000

The lists have to be the same length, because the i-th element of every list together makes up row i. If the lengths differ, pandas raises an error right away instead of padding anything for you.

One row per element: a list of dicts

If the data comes from an API or from a loop, the natural shape is the other way round - one list where each element is a record. pandas accepts that shape directly:

import pandas as pd

rows = [
    {"name": "Keyboard", "price": 450000},
    {"name": "Mouse", "price": 180000},
    {"name": "Monitor", "price": 2500000},
]
products = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(products)
print(products.index.tolist())
       name    price
0  Keyboard   450000
1     Mouse   180000
2   Monitor  2500000
[0, 1, 2]

Same table, two ways of writing it. Which one you pick depends on the shape your data already has; neither is more "correct" than the other.

The default index is not a row number

If you don't declare an index, pandas numbers the rows 0, 1, 2… It looks a lot like a row number, but only the first time round:

import pandas as pd

products = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["Keyboard", "Mouse", "Monitor"],
    "price": [450000, 180000, 2500000],
})
by_price = products.sort_values("price")
print(by_price)
print(by_price.index.tolist())
       name    price
1     Mouse   180000
0  Keyboard   450000
2   Monitor  2500000
[1, 0, 2]

The mouse moved to the top of the table but still carries the label 1. The index sticks to a row like a name; it is not renumbered to match the new position. Getting this early saves you the surprise later, when a table you have sorted or filtered shows row labels that jump around.

lessons.title: Reading CSV data into a table
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 4: Reading CSV data into a table

theory.contentHtml:
Typing lists by hand gets you three rows; the file exported from the sales system has three thousand. CSV data - one record per line, cells separated by commas - is read straight into a table by pd.read_csv.

In this course the data sits inside the lesson itself, as a string. read_csv only accepts something it can read like a file, so we wrap the string in io.StringIO to make it "look like a file":

import io
import pandas as pd

csv_text = """order_id,city,amount
1,Ha Noi,120000
2,Da Nang,90000
3,Ha Noi,150000
"""
orders = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text))
print(orders)
   order_id     city  amount
0         1   Ha Noi  120000
1         2  Da Nang   90000
2         3   Ha Noi  150000

In real life you change exactly one thing: pd.read_csv("orders.csv"), and everything else is identical. The first line of the CSV becomes the column names, and pandas infers a type for each column - order_id and amount come out as numbers, so you can do arithmetic on them straight away with no conversion.

Three parameters you will keep reaching for

Real files are rarely as clean as the example above. The separator is sometimes a semicolon, empty cells are sometimes written with a symbol of their own, and a date column is just a string by default:

import io
import pandas as pd

csv_text = """order_id;order_date;amount
1;2026-01-05;120000
2;2026-01-06;-
3;2026-01-06;150000
"""
orders = pd.read_csv(
    io.StringIO(csv_text),
    sep=";",
    na_values=["-"],
    parse_dates=["order_date"],
)
print(orders)
   order_id order_date    amount
0         1 2026-01-05  120000.0
1         2 2026-01-06       NaN
2         3 2026-01-06  150000.0

sep=";" says what the separator is. na_values=["-"] declares which symbols should be read as empty cells, and such a cell becomes NaN - that is why the amount column turns into floating point, since NaN is a float value. parse_dates turns the listed column into real dates, which is what lets you compare them or slice by month later; the string "2026-01-05" can only be compared the way text is compared.

lessons.title: A quick look at an unfamiliar table
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 5: A quick look at an unfamiliar table

theory.contentHtml:
Someone sends you a file and says "have a look at this for me". Before computing anything you need to answer three questions: how big is the table, what columns does it have, and what range are the numbers in. Three lines are enough:

import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho"],
    "amount": [120000, 90000, 150000, 200000, 80000, 110000],
    "quantity": [2, 1, 3, 4, 1, 2],
})
print(sales.shape)
print(sales.columns.tolist())
print(sales.head(3))
(6, 3)
['city', 'amount', 'quantity']
      city  amount  quantity
0   Ha Noi  120000         2
1  Da Nang   90000         1
2  Can Tho  150000         3

shape returns the pair (row count, column count) - six rows and three columns here. columns gives the column names in the order they currently sit. head(3) prints the first three rows so you can see what the real data looks like; tail(3) prints the last three, which helps when a file has a totals row or junk at the bottom. With no number passed, both take 5 rows.

describe(): the distribution of the numeric columns

import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho"],
    "amount": [120000, 90000, 150000, 200000, 80000, 110000],
    "quantity": [2, 1, 3, 4, 1, 2],
})
print(sales.describe())
              amount  quantity
count       6.000000  6.000000
mean   125000.000000  2.166667
std     44158.804332  1.169045
min     80000.000000  1.000000
25%     95000.000000  1.250000
50%    115000.000000  2.000000
75%    142500.000000  2.750000
max    200000.000000  4.000000

Only numeric columns are summarized, so city does not show up. count is the number of cells that hold a value - lower than the row count means that column has empty cells, and this is the cheapest way to spot missing data. 50% is the median; comparing it against mean tells you whether a few large values are dragging the distribution sideways. min and max are the ones that usually expose the absurd: a negative quantity, a price of 0, a birth year of 1900.

Once you have looked at these three things, you know enough to ask the data your next question.

lessons.title: Selecting one column and several columns
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 7: Selecting one column and several columns

theory.contentHtml:
The sales table has three columns but the report only needs two. You take columns out of a table with square brackets, and how many brackets you use decides what you get back:

import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho"],
    "amount": [120000, 90000, 150000],
    "quantity": [2, 1, 3],
})
print(sales["amount"])
0    120000
1     90000
2    150000
Name: amount, dtype: int64

One column name inside one pair of brackets gives you a Series: a sequence of values carrying the table's index, plus a Name line recording which column it came from. This is the shape you want when you are about to compute on that column, for example sales["amount"].sum().

For several columns, pass a list

import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho"],
    "amount": [120000, 90000, 150000],
    "quantity": [2, 1, 3],
})
print(sales[["city", "amount"]])
      city  amount
0   Ha Noi  120000
1  Da Nang   90000
2  Can Tho  150000

The result is a DataFrame holding exactly those two columns, ordered the way you wrote them in the list rather than the way they sit in the original table.

Why two sets of brackets

There is no separate syntax for "several columns". The outer square brackets are the selection itself, and what sits inside them is ["city", "amount"] - an ordinary Python list. A single name and pandas reads it as asking for one column, returning a Series; a list of names and pandas reads it as asking for a group of columns, returning a table.

One consequence is that you can ask for a single column and still get a DataFrame back:

import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho"],
    "amount": [120000, 90000, 150000],
    "quantity": [2, 1, 3],
})
print(type(sales["amount"]).__name__)
print(type(sales[["amount"]]).__name__)
print(sales[["amount"]])
Series
DataFrame
   amount
0  120000
1   90000
2  150000

Same data, two shapes. Pick the shape that fits the job: take the Series when you need a sequence of numbers to compute with, take the DataFrame when you need a table to join onto something else or write out to a file.

lessons.title: Renaming, reordering and dropping columns
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 8: Renaming, reordering and dropping columns

theory.contentHtml:
Files exported from a spreadsheet tend to carry column names like Product Name, Unit Price, QTY - spaces, capitalization all over the place, abbreviations. Typing those all afternoon is tiring and easy to get wrong, so the first job is usually to rename them:

import pandas as pd

raw = pd.DataFrame({
    "Product Name": ["Keyboard", "Mouse"],
    "Unit Price": [450000, 180000],
    "QTY": [2, 5],
})
clean = raw.rename(columns={"Product Name": "product", "Unit Price": "price", "QTY": "quantity"})
print(clean)
print(raw.columns.tolist())
    product   price  quantity
0  Keyboard  450000         2
1     Mouse  180000         5
['Product Name', 'Unit Price', 'QTY']

rename takes a dict of old-name to new-name and only touches the keys you list; a column you don't mention keeps its name, and a name that doesn't exist in the table is ignored rather than raising an error. The last line shows the original table is unchanged: rename returns a new table, so to keep the result you have to assign it to a variable.

Reordering the columns

There is no dedicated function for this - you re-select the columns in the order you want, using the multi-column selection from the previous lesson:

import pandas as pd

clean = pd.DataFrame({
    "product": ["Keyboard", "Mouse"],
    "price": [450000, 180000],
    "quantity": [2, 5],
})
print(clean[["product", "quantity", "price"]])
    product  quantity   price
0  Keyboard         2  450000
1     Mouse         5  180000

This doubles as dropping columns: any column whose name is not in the list does not come along. The downside is that you have to name every column you want to keep - on a thirty-column table where you only want one gone, that is a lot of typing.

Dropping columns with drop

import pandas as pd

clean = pd.DataFrame({
    "product": ["Keyboard", "Mouse"],
    "price": [450000, 180000],
    "quantity": [2, 5],
    "note": ["", "gift"],
})
print(clean.drop(columns=["note"]))
    product   price  quantity
0  Keyboard  450000         2
1     Mouse  180000         5

drop(columns=[...]) comes at it from the opposite side: name what has to go, and everything else stays as it was, content and order alike. Like rename, it returns a new table. A column name that isn't in the table makes drop raise an error - unlike rename - so this is the fragile spot when this month's input file is missing a column that last month's had.

lessons.title: Quiz Your first data table
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 10: Quiz Your first data table

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between a Series and a DataFrame?

options.label: A
options.text: A Series is for numbers, a DataFrame is for strings and dates

options.label: B
options.text: A Series always has exactly one row, a DataFrame has many rows

options.label: C
options.text: A Series is one labeled column, and a DataFrame gathers several such columns onto a shared index

options.label: D
options.text: A Series is read-only; to change a value you have to convert it to a DataFrame

questions.explanation: A Series is a sequence of values paired with a sequence of labels called the index, and a DataFrame is several such sequences side by side on the same set of row labels - which is why pulling one column out of a DataFrame gives you back exactly one Series carrying the table's index. Data type is not the line between them: a Series holding strings or dates is perfectly ordinary, and each column of a DataFrame keeps its own type. A Series is not limited to one row either, and neither of them is read-only - both can be modified.

questions.prompt: In pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Ha Noi", "Hue"], "amount": [120000, 90000]}), what does each key of the dict become?

options.label: A
options.text: A column, with the elements of the list being that column's values row by row

options.label: B
options.text: A row, with the elements of the list being the values of the columns on that row

options.label: C
options.text: An index label, with the lists being the table's only data

options.label: D
options.text: A sub-table, so the result is two small tables stitched together

questions.explanation: A dict of lists declares data column-wise: keys become column names, lists become that column's values from top to bottom, which is why the lists must be the same length - the i-th element of every list together makes up row i. To declare data row-wise you use the other shape, a list of dicts where each dict is one record. The index does not come from the dict keys; pandas numbers it 0, 1, 2 when you don't specify one, and the result is always a single table rather than several tables stitched together.

questions.prompt: A table has the default index 0, 1, 2. After sorting it by price ascending, which index label does the row now at the top carry?

options.label: A
options.text: Always 0, because pandas renumbers the index after every sort

options.label: B
options.text: A sorted table no longer has an index, only row numbers

options.label: C
options.text: There is no way to tell in advance, the index gets shuffled into a random order

options.label: D
options.text: That row's own old label, for example 1 if the cheapest row used to sit second

questions.explanation: The index sticks to a row like a name rather than counting positions, so sorting only moves the rows around while the labels travel with them - the cheapest row goes to the top still carrying its label 1. The fact that 0, 1, 2 looks like a row number only holds for a table you have just built and not touched. Every table always has an index, including after a sort or a filter, and the order of the labels is entirely predictable: it is the order of the rows after the sort.

questions.prompt: How do sales["amount"] and sales[["amount"]] differ?

options.label: A
options.text: They don't differ, the second pair of brackets is just a habit that reads more clearly

options.label: B
options.text: The first returns a Series, the second returns a DataFrame holding only the amount column

options.label: C
options.text: The first takes the amount column, the second takes the row labeled amount

options.label: D
options.text: The first returns a copy, the second returns a view onto the original table

questions.explanation: What sits inside the brackets decides the shape of the result: a single name and pandas reads it as asking for one column, returning a Series, while ["amount"] is a Python list, so pandas reads it as asking for a group of columns - a group of one is still a group, and the result is a one-column DataFrame. The second pair of brackets is therefore not decoration, the two forms produce two different types. Plain square brackets on a DataFrame read a name as a column name rather than a row label, and copy versus view is a topic of its own, not what separates these two.

questions.prompt: What does df.describe() show you by default?

options.label: A
options.text: The first five rows of the table, so you can see what the real data looks like

options.label: B
options.text: Each column name along with the description of its meaning recorded by whoever built the table

options.label: C
options.text: The number of rows and columns in the table, returned as a pair of numbers

options.label: D
options.text: A statistical summary of the numeric columns: count, mean, percentiles, minimum and maximum

questions.explanation: describe() summarizes the distribution of each numeric column, and the three numbers worth reading first are count (lower than the row count means the column has empty cells), min and max (they tend to expose impossible values), and 50% against mean to see whether the distribution is being pulled sideways. Text columns do not appear in this summary by default. Looking at a few rows of real data is head()'s job, the size of the table lives in shape, and a description of what each column means is something pandas does not have - it reads the data, not the intentions of whoever made the file.

questions.prompt: The table raw has four columns. You run raw.rename(columns={"QTY": "quantity"}) and then print raw. What happens?

options.label: A
options.text: raw raises an error because the dict names only one column while the table has four

options.label: B
options.text: raw has the column renamed in place, and the call returns None

options.label: C
options.text: raw still has the column QTY, because rename returns a new table instead of modifying the old one

options.label: D
options.text: raw renames QTY and also deletes the three columns not named in the dict

questions.explanation: rename belongs to the family of methods that return a new table, so if you don't assign the result anywhere the new table is thrown away and raw keeps its old names - this is the most common beginner mistake. Naming only one column in the dict is perfectly valid: a column not named keeps its name and stays in the table, and rename never deletes columns. It is forgiving enough that an old name which doesn't exist in the table is ignored rather than raising an error - unlike drop, which does raise when asked to remove a column that isn't there.

lessons.title: Three ways to pull data out brackets, .loc, .iloc
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 11: Three ways to pull data out brackets, .loc, .iloc

theory.contentHtml:
The orders table is already sitting in orders. The next step is always to pull a piece of it out: one column to total up, a few columns to export into a report, a single row to check. pandas has three ways in for those three needs, and picking the wrong one gives you a different answer.

Bare square brackets talk about columns:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103],
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 5],
})
print(orders["qty"])
print(orders[["order_id", "qty"]])
0    2
1    1
2    5
Name: qty, dtype: int64
   order_id  qty
0       101    2
1       102    1
2       103    5

A single column name gives you a Series - one column lifted out of the table. A list of column names gives you a smaller DataFrame, with the columns in the order you listed them rather than the order they sit in the original table. The two layers of brackets look confusing but there is a reason for them: the outer layer is the selection syntax, the inner one is just an ordinary Python list.

To take rows you have to say how you name them

.loc takes a label - the number printed in the leftmost column. .iloc takes a position, counting from 0. In the table we just built, labels and positions coincide, so both spellings land on the same row. One filter is enough to pull them apart:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104],
    "city": ["Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 5, 3],
})
hanoi = orders[orders["city"] == "Ha Noi"]
print(hanoi)
print(hanoi.loc[1, "order_id"])
print(hanoi["order_id"].iloc[1])
   order_id    city  qty
1       102  Ha Noi    1
2       103  Ha Noi    5
102
103

hanoi has only two rows left but it still carries labels 1 and 2 from the old table - pandas does not renumber after a filter. So .loc[1] goes looking for the row labelled 1, which is the first row of hanoi, and returns 102; .iloc[1] counts to the second position and returns 103.

Which one to reach for

A label sticks to its row and follows it for life, even after the table is filtered or sorted. A position changes every time the table changes shape. When you say "the order numbered 103" you are talking about a label; when you say "the first three rows" you are talking about a position. Write down the one you actually mean and your code still does the right thing after somebody slips an extra filtering step into the middle.

lessons.title: Filtering rows with a TrueFalse mask
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 13: Filtering rows with a TrueFalse mask

theory.contentHtml:
Your manager asks: which orders have three items or more? In plain Python you would write a loop and an if. pandas does not go that way - it compares the whole column in one shot:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104],
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 5, 3],
})
mask = orders["qty"] >= 3
print(mask)
print(orders[mask])
0    False
1    False
2     True
3     True
Name: qty, dtype: bool
   order_id     city  qty
2       103   Ha Noi    5
3       104  Can Tho    3

The comparison does not hand back one true/false answer, it hands back one answer per row: a Series of True/False values, exactly as long as the table and carrying the same row labels. That is what a mask is. Give the mask to the square brackets and pandas keeps the rows that line up with True. Labels - not order - are what pandas uses to line the mask up with the table, which is why a mask computed from one table cannot be used to filter another.

Combining conditions: &, | and ~, always with parentheses

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104],
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 5, 3],
})
print(orders[(orders["qty"] >= 3) & (orders["city"] == "Ha Noi")])
print(orders[~(orders["city"] == "Ha Noi")])
   order_id    city  qty
2       103  Ha Noi    5
   order_id     city  qty
1       102  Da Nang    1
3       104  Can Tho    3

& means "and", | means "or", ~ negates. The parentheses around each side are not there to look tidy: in Python, & binds more tightly than >= and ==, so drop them and 3 & orders["city"] gets evaluated first, handing you a type error somewhere that has nothing to do with what you meant.

Why and does not work

Swap & for and and pandas raises "The truth value of a Series is ambiguous". and is a Python operator; it needs each side to collapse into one true/false value so it can decide which side to return. Each side here is a four-element Series with some True and some False - there is no way to collapse that into a single value without guessing, and pandas refuses to guess. & compares element by element and returns a new Series of the same length. For the same reason, or has to be written | and not has to be written ~.

lessons.title: isin, between, query conditions written to be read
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 15: isin, between, query conditions written to be read

theory.contentHtml:
Write the condition "the city is one of the northern ones" with | and it turns into a long train: (orders["city"] == "Ha Noi") | (orders["city"] == "Hai Phong") | .... Each new city is another clause, and reading it back three months later means tracing every parenthesis. pandas ships two helpers for the two shapes of condition you meet most often.

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104, 105],
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Hue", "Can Tho", "Ha Noi"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 5, 3, 8],
})
print(orders[orders["city"].isin(["Ha Noi", "Hai Phong"])])
print(orders[orders["qty"].between(2, 5)])
   order_id    city  qty
0       101  Ha Noi    2
4       105  Ha Noi    8
   order_id     city  qty
0       101   Ha Noi    2
2       103      Hue    5
3       104  Can Tho    3

isin takes a list and asks each row "is your value in here?". A value that does not exist in the table, like "Hai Phong", causes no error - it simply matches nothing, which is what lets you keep one shared configuration list across several different tables. between(2, 5) asks "is it inside the range?", and both ends count: the row with qty 2 and the row with qty 5 are both kept. For a range open at both ends, add inclusive="neither".

query: the whole condition packed into a string

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104, 105],
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Hue", "Can Tho", "Ha Noi"],
    "qty": [2, 1, 5, 3, 8],
})
print(orders.query("qty >= 3 and city != 'Da Nang'"))
   order_id     city  qty
2       103      Hue    5
3       104  Can Tho    3
4       105   Ha Noi    8

Inside that string the column names are written bare, with no orders["..."] repeated in every clause, and and/or/not work again because pandas parses the string itself instead of leaving it to Python. String values inside are wrapped in single quotes so they do not collide with the double quotes around the whole thing.

Which one to use

For one or two clauses a mask is still the shortest thing to write. For a list of values reach for isin; for a numeric range or a date range, between. query reads best once the condition runs to four or five clauses, but the trade-off is that it lives in a string: misspell a column name and you only hear about it at run time, with no help from the editor.

lessons.title: Editing a filtered table when it lands and when it doesn't
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 16: Editing a filtered table when it lands and when it doesn't

theory.contentHtml:
The orders table carries a shipping fee per city. You filter out the Ha Noi orders to make shipping free for that group, make the edit, then go back to the original table to check:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi"],
    "ship_fee": [30000, 25000, 30000],
})
hanoi = orders[orders["city"] == "Ha Noi"]
hanoi["ship_fee"] = 0
print(orders)
      city  ship_fee
0   Ha Noi     30000
1  Da Nang     25000
2   Ha Noi     30000

Not one cell of the original table changed. The edit went into hanoi - a different table - and stayed there. pandas does say something: it prints a SettingWithCopyWarning with the line "A value is trying to be set on a copy of a slice from a DataFrame", but the warning slides past among dozens of lines of output so it is very easy to miss, and the code carries on running as normal.

The other direction is worse

Pull one column out as a Series and edit that, and this time the edit really does land:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi"],
    "ship_fee": [30000, 25000, 30000],
})
fees = orders["ship_fee"]
fees.iloc[0] = 0
print(orders)
      city  ship_fee
0   Ha Noi         0
1  Da Nang     25000
2   Ha Noi     30000

The two snippets look the same in intent and come out opposite: one loses the edit, the other edits the original data by accident. The reason is that pandas sometimes returns a copy and sometimes returns a view onto the same block of memory, and where that line falls depends on how you pulled the data out, not on what you wanted.

Worth noticing: both snippets print the same warning while ending up in opposite places. So do not read the warning as a diagnosis - all it says is that this spot is ambiguous, not where your edit went.

Don't guess: say it outright with .loc or .copy()

To edit the original table, fold the condition and the column into a single .loc call instead of splitting it into two steps:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi"],
    "ship_fee": [30000, 25000, 30000],
})
orders.loc[orders["city"] == "Ha Noi", "ship_fee"] = 0
print(orders)
      city  ship_fee
0   Ha Noi         0
1  Da Nang     25000
2   Ha Noi         0

And if what you want is a table of your own to play with freely, write .copy() at the moment you filter: hanoi = orders[orders["city"] == "Ha Noi"].copy(). From there hanoi lives independently, nothing you do to it echoes back to the original table, and the warning disappears too.

One note for when you run this on your own machine: as of pandas 3.0, Copy-on-Write is enabled by default and the second snippet above no longer reaches the original table. This course's sandbox runs pandas 2.2, so what you see is the old behaviour - which is also the behaviour you will meet in most projects currently running. The rule of one .loc call, and .copy() when you need a table of your own, holds on both versions.

lessons.title: Sorting a table and taking the top rows
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 18: Sorting a table and taking the top rows

theory.contentHtml:
The orders table has four rows and your manager asks which order is the biggest. With four rows you can see it by eye; with four thousand you have to sort:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104],
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho"],
    "amount": [240000, 150000, 600000, 330000],
})
print(orders.sort_values("amount", ascending=False))
   order_id     city  amount
2       103   Ha Noi  600000
3       104  Can Tho  330000
0       101   Ha Noi  240000
1       102  Da Nang  150000

Leave ascending=False out and the default is ascending - the piece people forget most often, and it fails quietly: you still get a table, just the wrong way up. Notice that the label column now reads 2, 3, 0, 1: labels travel with their rows instead of staying put, so the first row of the table no longer carries label 0.

Several keys, and a shortcut for the top rows

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104],
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho"],
    "amount": [240000, 150000, 600000, 240000],
})
print(orders.sort_values(["city", "amount"], ascending=[True, False]))
print(orders.nlargest(2, "amount"))
   order_id     city  amount
3       104  Can Tho  240000
1       102  Da Nang  150000
2       103   Ha Noi  600000
0       101   Ha Noi  240000
   order_id    city  amount
2       103  Ha Noi  600000
0       101  Ha Noi  240000

Pass a list of column names and pandas sorts by the first column, only looking at the next one where the first one ties - here that is city A→Z, and within each city the amount descending. ascending takes a list too, so each column can go its own way.

When you only need a few rows off the top, nlargest(2, "amount") states the intent more directly than sorting the whole table and slicing, and nsmallest covers the other direction. Notice how it settles ties: two orders both at 240000, and it keeps the one that appears first in the original table. If you want ties settled by some other criterion, you have to go back to sort_values.

After sorting, renumber

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103, 104],
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho"],
    "amount": [240000, 150000, 600000, 330000],
})
top = orders.sort_values("amount", ascending=False).head(2).reset_index(drop=True)
print(top)
   order_id     city  amount
0       103   Ha Noi  600000
1       104  Can Tho  330000

For a ranking table headed into a report, the old labels only get in the way. reset_index(drop=True) renumbers from 0; without drop=True, pandas keeps the old labels around as a new column named index.

questions.prompt: What does df[df["qty"] > 3] return?

options.label: A
options.text: A Series holding a True/False value for each row of the table

options.label: B
options.text: A DataFrame containing only the rows where qty is greater than 3

options.label: C
options.text: A DataFrame containing only the qty column, with values below 3 filtered out

options.label: D
options.text: The number of rows that satisfy the condition, that is, a single number

questions.explanation: The expression inside the brackets, df["qty"] > 3, produces a Series of True/False values - that is the mask. Give that mask to the DataFrame's brackets and pandas keeps the rows that line up with True, returning a DataFrame with all of its columns, not just qty. The True/False Series is the result of the comparison, not of the filtering, and to find out how many rows qualify you have to count them separately, for example with len() or .sum() on the mask.

questions.prompt: Table df has the default index 0, 1, 2… What is the difference between df.loc[2] and df.iloc[2]?

options.label: A
options.text: loc only works on columns while iloc only works on rows

options.label: B
options.text: No difference at all - the two spellings give the same result on every table

options.label: C
options.text: loc looks up by index label, iloc counts by position - they coincide on this table but drift apart after a filter or a sort

options.label: D
options.text: loc returns a copy while iloc returns a view, a difference in memory rather than in which row you get

questions.explanation: With the default index, labels and positions happen to coincide, so both spellings land on the same row and newcomers easily take them for one thing. The difference shows up the moment the table is filtered or sorted: the index travels with the rows instead of being renumbered, so a filtered table may well start at label 5 - at which point df.loc[2] looks for the row labelled 2 and errors out if it is gone, while df.iloc[2] still gives you the third row counting from the top. Both work on rows and columns alike, and the view-versus-copy question is a separate story, not what tells these two apart.

questions.prompt: To take the rows where qty is greater than 3 and city equals "Ha Noi", how do you write it?

options.label: A
options.text: df[(df["qty"] > 3) & (df["city"] == "Ha Noi")]

options.label: B
options.text: df[df["qty"] > 3 and df["city"] == "Ha Noi"]

options.label: C
options.text: df[df["qty"] > 3, df["city"] == "Ha Noi"]

options.label: D
options.text: df[df["qty"] > 3][df["city"] == "Ha Noi"]

questions.explanation: Joining two masks calls for &, and each side has to sit inside parentheses because & binds more tightly than the comparisons - leave them out and pandas reads the order wrong and raises an error. Python's and keyword is no use here: it demands that each side collapse into a single true/false value, while each side is a whole Series, so pandas raises an error telling you to use &. The comma-separated spelling is .loc syntax, not bare-bracket syntax. And filtering twice in a row computes the second mask on the original table while applying it to the filtered one, so the lengths do not match.

questions.prompt: You write sub = df[df["city"] == "Ha Noi"] and then sub["ship_fee"] = 0. What happens in this course's sandbox?

options.label: A
options.text: df is updated exactly as hoped, with no warning at all

options.label: B
options.text: The program stops with an error because writing into a filtered table is not allowed

options.label: C
options.text: sub changes but df does not, along with a SettingWithCopyWarning

options.label: D
options.text: Neither sub nor df changes - the assignment is skipped entirely

questions.explanation: The filter returns a table of its own, so the assignment goes into that separate table: sub gets the new values while df stays put - exactly the kind of bug that loses an edit without anyone noticing. pandas does warn, with SettingWithCopyWarning, but it is only a warning: the program keeps running rather than stopping, so it slips by easily. To edit df, fold the condition and the column into a single .loc call.

questions.prompt: fees = df["ship_fee"] and then fees.iloc[0] = 0. What happens to df in this course's sandbox?

options.label: A
options.text: df changes too, because fees looks at the same data as the column in the table

options.label: B
options.text: df is unchanged, because pulling out a column always creates an independent copy

options.label: C
options.text: df is unchanged, but only when the table has more than one numeric column

options.label: D
options.text: The program raises an error because a Series taken from a table does not allow assignment

questions.explanation: Pulling out a column usually gives you a Series that looks straight at the table's own memory, so writing into that Series writes into the table - the exact opposite of the row-filtering case in the previous question, and the reason to state your intent outright instead of guessing. The assignment is perfectly legal, no error is raised, and the number of columns in the table has nothing to do with it. If you want a detached column to play with, add .copy() at the moment you pull it out.

questions.prompt: You need the three highest-revenue orders. Which spelling is the shortest and clearest?

options.label: A
options.text: df.sort_values("revenue").head(3)

options.label: B
options.text: df.nlargest(3, "revenue")

options.label: C
options.text: df[df["revenue"] > df["revenue"].mean()].head(3)

options.label: D
options.text: df.max()[:3]

questions.explanation: nlargest states outright what needs doing - take the largest few rows, by this column - so reading the code back tells you immediately. Sorting and then taking the top also gives the right answer, but only with ascending=False added: written the way the other option has it, sort_values goes ascending and you get the three smallest orders. Filtering by the mean returns the above-average orders rather than the top three, and how many rows that is depends on the data. As for df.max(), it collapses each column into a single value, so slicing three elements off it gives three disconnected numbers that are no longer any order at all.

lessons.title: Missing cells spot them before you compute
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 21: Missing cells spot them before you compute

theory.contentHtml:
A survey form lets people skip a few questions. You download the results, work out the average study hours, and the number comes out nothing like what you got on paper:

import pandas as pd

responses = pd.DataFrame({
    "student": ["An", "Binh", "Chi", "Dung"],
    "hours": [4.0, None, 6.0, 3.0],
    "score": [8.0, 7.5, None, 9.0],
})
print(responses)
print(round(responses["hours"].mean(), 2))
  student  hours  score
0      An    4.0    8.0
1    Binh    NaN    7.5
2     Chi    6.0    NaN
3    Dung    3.0    9.0
4.33

Binh's empty cell shows up as NaN - short for "not a number", pandas' standard marker for a cell with no data. By hand you get (4 + 6 + 3) / 4 = 3.25, but mean() returns 4.33 because it skips the missing cell: it adds three numbers and divides by 3, not by 4. The denominator changed and nothing said a word.

Counting missing cells per column

isna() asks every cell a single question: is this one missing?

import pandas as pd

responses = pd.DataFrame({
    "student": ["An", "Binh", "Chi", "Dung"],
    "hours": [4.0, None, 6.0, 3.0],
    "score": [8.0, 7.5, None, 9.0],
})
print(responses.isna())
print(responses.isna().sum())
   student  hours  score
0    False  False  False
1    False   True  False
2    False  False   True
3    False  False  False
student    0
hours      1
score      1
dtype: int64

The full True/False table is only readable while the data is small. Summing it down each column counts True as 1, so isna().sum() hands you the number of missing cells per column - this is the first line worth typing when you open an unfamiliar dataset.

Why you count first and decide after

That number changes the whole approach. A column missing 1 cell out of 400 loses nothing if you drop those rows. A column missing 300 out of 400 loses three quarters of the table if you drop them, and if instead you fill those 300 cells with some convenient value, every statistic afterwards mostly reflects the value you made up. Counting also shows you where the gaps cluster: if score is only blank for students who just joined, dropping those rows erases the whole group of new students from the report.

theory.contentHtml:
An orders table has a customer column that is occasionally blank, and a note column that is blank most of the time because the note is optional. You want to tidy the table up, and dropna() is the first thing that comes to mind:

    "customer": ["An", None, "Chi", "Dung"],
    "note": ["gift", None, None, "urgent"],

print(orders.dropna(subset=["customer"]))

3         4     Dung  urgent
   order_id customer    note
0         1       An    gift
2         3      Chi    None
3         4     Dung  urgent

Called bare, dropna() removes every row with at least one empty cell in any column - order 3 disappears purely because nobody wrote a note. The subset argument narrows what counts: only a missing customer is a reason to drop the row, an empty note is ignored. On a real table the gap between those two calls is usually a few thousand rows.

Notice that the empty cell in note prints as None, not as the NaN you saw in the numeric column. A text column keeps exactly what you handed it, which here is Python's None; a numeric column turns every gap into NaN. Two markers, one meaning - "no data" - and isna() catches both, which is why you ask isna() instead of comparing with == None.

Filling keeps the row, but fills it with what

fillna() goes the other way: it keeps every row and plugs the gaps with a value you pick. The hard part is the picking.

import pandas as pd

scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "student": ["An", "Binh", "Chi", "Dung", "Em"],
    "score": [8.0, 9.0, None, 7.0, None],
})
print(round(scores["score"].mean(), 2))
print(round(scores["score"].fillna(0).mean(), 2))
print(round(scores["score"].fillna(scores["score"].median()).mean(), 2))
8.0
4.8
8.0

Filling with 0 drags the average from 8.0 down to 4.8 - you have just declared that both absent students scored zero. Filling with the median of the scores you do have leaves the average sitting at 8.0: you add no information, but you invent no wrong information either. For a numeric column the median is usually safer than the mean, because a handful of extreme values cannot pull it around.

Which one to choose

Drop the row when the missing cell is the thing that makes the whole row useless: an order with no order id, a transaction with no amount. Fill when the gap has an obvious default meaning - a blank discount means no discount was given, so writing 0 records the truth rather than guessing at it. And when the gap sits in the middle of a measured column with no default meaning available, remember that every value you fill in is a value you added yourself, and the statistics that follow will look more certain than the data actually allows.

lessons.rawTitle: Bài 25: Duplicate records and the business key

theory.contentHtml:
You export orders from the web sales system and from the app sales system, then stack the two files together. Order 101 was sold on the web but it also got recorded in the other file, so it sits in the table twice and revenue quietly swells:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 101, 103],
    "channel": ["web", "app", "web", "web"],
    "amount": [250, 400, 250, 180],
})
print(orders.duplicated())
print(orders.drop_duplicates())
0    False
1    False
2     True
3    False
dtype: bool
   order_id channel  amount
0       101     web     250
1       102     app     400
3       103     web     180

duplicated() marks True on a row that has appeared before, so the first row of each group is always False. To find out how many extra rows the table carries, orders.duplicated().sum(). drop_duplicates() keeps the first row and removes the repeats; index 2 is gone from the result, and that is the sign that a row was dropped rather than the table being renumbered.

Duplicates by business key, not by whole row

By default pandas calls two rows duplicates only when every column matches. Real tables are rarely that tidy: the same order exported from two systems usually differs in a timestamp or a status column, so nothing counts as a duplicate even though both rows clearly describe one order.

import pandas as pd

events = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 101, 102],
    "status": ["pending", "paid", "paid"],
    "updated_at": ["2026-01-05", "2026-01-07", "2026-01-06"],
})
print(events.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"], keep="first"))
print(events.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"], keep="last"))
   order_id   status  updated_at
0       101  pending  2026-01-05
2       102     paid  2026-01-06
   order_id status  updated_at
1       101   paid  2026-01-07
2       102   paid  2026-01-06

subset=["order_id"] says the order id is what identifies a record - that is the business key. And keep picks which row stays: "first" keeps the first, "last" keeps the last, False throws away every row involved in a duplicate.

keep counts table order, not time

This is where people slip. keep="last" has no idea what updated_at means; it simply keeps whichever row stands last in the table's current order. In the example above the two happen to coincide, so the answer is right. If the export comes out in another order, the last row is the older record and you keep the stale status with no warning at all. To actually keep the newest version you have to sort_values on the time column first, and only then drop duplicates.

lessons.title: A numeric column read as text
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 27: A numeric column read as text

theory.contentHtml:
A CSV exported from the sales system has one cell reading unknown in the amount column. One cell, but it is enough for pandas to conclude that the whole amount column is text rather than numbers, and addition changes meaning:

import io
import pandas as pd

csv_text = """order_id,amount
101,250
102,400
103,unknown
"""
orders = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text))
print(orders["amount"].tolist())
print(orders["amount"].sum())
['250', '400', 'unknown']
250400unknown

sum() raises nothing; it glues the three strings together. This is the dangerous kind of breakage, because the program keeps running and still prints something that looks like an answer. The cheapest way to catch it is to try one operation and look: if the sum comes out as a long string, or multiplying by 2 repeats the value instead of doubling it, the column is text. tolist() tells you straight away too - numbers print bare, strings print with quotes.

Clean column: astype is enough

When every cell is a valid number, astype converts in one step:

import pandas as pd

prices = pd.Series(["250", "400", "180"])
print((prices.astype(int) * 2).tolist())
[500, 800, 360]

But astype does not forgive. Hand it unknown and it stops the whole program:

# ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'unknown'
orders["amount"].astype(int)

Column with broken cells: to_numeric with errors="coerce"

Real data is rarely clean, and you usually do not want a whole pipeline to die over one cell. pd.to_numeric with errors="coerce" turns the unreadable cells into NaN instead of raising:

import io
import pandas as pd

csv_text = """order_id,amount
101,250
102,400
103,unknown
"""
orders = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text))
orders["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(orders["amount"], errors="coerce")
print(orders)
print(orders["amount"].sum())
   order_id  amount
0       101   250.0
1       102   400.0
2       103     NaN
650.0

The broken cell becomes NaN and sum() returns 650.0 - a real number, added from the two orders that parsed. The column comes out as floats rather than integers, because NaN can only live in a float column. The nice thing about coerce is that it funnels everything broken into one shape you already know how to handle: after this step, isna().sum() tells you how many cells failed, and you are back to the drop-or-fill choice from the previous lesson.

lessons.title: Hand-typed strings
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 29: Hand-typed strings

theory.contentHtml:
The signup form lets people type their city themselves. You count how many signups came from Ha Noi and get back 0, while your own eyes can see three rows:

import pandas as pd

signups = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": [" Ha Noi", "ha noi", "HA NOI ", "Da Nang"],
})
print(signups["city"].tolist())
print((signups["city"] == "Ha Noi").sum())
[' Ha Noi', 'ha noi', 'HA NOI ', 'Da Nang']
0

tolist() shows the culprits: one row has a leading space, one has a trailing space, one is all lowercase. A computer compares strings character by character, so those three variants are three different values - and all three differ from the "Ha Noi" you wrote in the condition. This is not a rare case: whenever a human typed the data, assume from the start that spacing and capitalisation vary.

Trim the spaces, settle on one case

A string Series has a door of its own called .str, which opens up string operations that run on every cell:

import pandas as pd

signups = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": [" Ha Noi", "ha noi", "HA NOI ", "Da Nang"],
})
clean = signups["city"].str.strip().str.lower()
print(clean.tolist())
print(clean.value_counts())
['ha noi', 'ha noi', 'ha noi', 'da nang']
city
ha noi     3
da nang    1
Name: count, dtype: int64

.str.strip() cuts the whitespace off both ends, .str.lower() folds everything to lowercase, and the two chain because each step returns a new Series. Then value_counts() groups identical values and counts them, already sorted from most to fewest - it is the short form of grouping by value and counting, which you will meet in full with groupby in a later module.

Note that lowercase is not a mandatory convention; what is mandatory is that every cell ends up in the same case. lower() gets the nod because it is never ambiguous.

Find, replace, split

Three more everyday jobs, all through .str:

import pandas as pd

products = pd.DataFrame({
    "code": ["SKU-101-red", "SKU-102-blue", "SKU-103-red"],
})
print(products["code"].str.contains("red").tolist())
print(products["code"].str.replace("SKU-", "", regex=False).tolist())
print(products["code"].str.split("-").tolist())
[True, False, True]
['101-red', '102-blue', '103-red']
[['SKU', '101', 'red'], ['SKU', '102', 'blue'], ['SKU', '103', 'red']]

contains returns a True/False mask you can feed straight into row filtering, exactly as in the previous module. replace with regex=False replaces the literal text you handed it - leave the default and characters like . or ( get read as regular-expression syntax. split cuts each cell into a list at the separator.

lessons.title: Quiz Cleaning data
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 31: Quiz Cleaning data

questions.prompt: A table has a price column and a qty column, and one row is missing qty. After computing df["price"] * df["qty"], what does the result cell for that row hold?

options.label: A
options.text: 0, because pandas treats a missing cell as an empty value

options.label: B
options.text: The price itself, because the missing side is skipped in the multiplication

options.label: C
options.text: NaN, because one side of the multiplication is undefined

options.label: D
options.text: No cell at all - that row is dropped from the result of the multiplication

questions.explanation: The arithmetic runs row by row, and multiplying a number by something undefined leaves the answer undefined, so that cell becomes NaN while the rest of the column computes as normal. The easy confusion is that column-wide functions such as mean() or sum() skip missing cells instead of spreading NaN - two different behaviours over the same data. pandas does not quietly read a missing cell as 0 (that would invent a number), and it does not silently throw the row away either: the result always has as many rows as the input.

questions.prompt: A 400-row table: note is an optional comment so 300 of its cells are blank, while amount is blank in only 2. What happens when you call df.dropna()?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the 2 rows missing amount are dropped, because note is an optional column

options.label: B
options.text: Every row missing at least one cell is dropped, so the 300 rows with no note go too

options.label: C
options.text: The note column is removed from the table because it is blank in more than half the rows

options.label: D
options.text: The row count stays the same and the blank cells are filled with the value from the row above

questions.explanation: Called bare, dropna() looks at every column and removes a row the moment it sees any blank cell, so one optional comment column is enough to erase three quarters of the table. The fix is dropna(subset=["amount"]), so that only genuinely required columns are grounds for dropping a row. dropna() works on rows and never decides to remove a column on its own, and it fills nothing - plugging gaps is fillna()'s job.

questions.prompt: An event table has several rows for the same order_id, each row carrying a different status. To leave one row per order, namely the row that stands last in the table, what do you write?

options.label: A
options.text: df.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id", "status"], keep="last")

options.label: B
options.text: df.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])

options.label: C
options.text: df.drop_duplicates(keep="last")

options.label: D
options.text: df.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"], keep="last")

questions.explanation: You need both arguments: subset says the order id is what identifies a record, and keep picks which row survives. Adding status to subset breaks it immediately, because every order-id–status pair becomes a record of its own and the question says each row carries a different status, so nothing gets dropped at all. Leaving subset out does the same thing: pandas compares all the columns and again finds no duplicates. With subset but no keep, the default is "first", which keeps the first row - the opposite of what was asked. And remember that "last" only means last in the table's current order, so keeping the newest record means sorting by time first.

questions.prompt: An amount column read from CSV has one cell holding "unknown". What does pd.to_numeric(df["amount"], errors="coerce") do to that column?

options.label: A
options.text: Turns the broken cell into NaN and the remaining cells into numbers

options.label: B
options.text: Leaves the string "unknown" in place and converts only the readable cells to numbers

options.label: C
options.text: Replaces the broken cell with 0 and converts the whole column to integers

options.label: D
options.text: Raises ValueError right at the broken cell and stops the program

questions.explanation: coerce means convert no matter what: any cell that does not read as a number becomes NaN, and the column turns into a float column (because NaN can only live among floats). That funnels everything broken into a single shape you already know how to handle with isna(), dropna() or fillna(). A column cannot be half number and half string, so leaving "unknown" in place is impossible; replacing it with 0 invents a zero-value transaction instead of marking the data as missing; and raising is the behaviour of errors="raise" - precisely the default that coerce was introduced to replace.

questions.prompt: A city column holds city names typed in by users. To trim the stray whitespace off both ends of every cell, what do you write?

options.label: A
options.text: df["city"].strip()

options.label: B
options.text: df["city"].str.strip()

options.label: C
options.text: df["city"].replace(" ", "")

options.label: D
options.text: df.strip("city")

questions.explanation: Python's string operations work on one string, while here you have a whole column, so pandas gathers them behind .str to apply cell by cell and return a new Series. Drop the .str and the Series has no strip method at all, which is an attribute error; df.strip(...) is further off still, since a DataFrame has no such thing either. The replace option is wrong twice over: a Series' replace matches the whole value rather than searching inside the string, and even if it did match, deleting every space would turn "Ha Noi" into "HaNoi" - not what you wanted.

questions.prompt: A signup table has hand-typed city values (" Ha Noi", "ha noi", "HA NOI ") and duplicate records on the email–city pair. You need the number of signups per city. Which order of steps makes sense?

options.label: A
options.text: Drop the duplicates first, then normalise the strings, then count

options.label: B
options.text: Count first to see the scale, then normalise the strings, then drop the duplicates

options.label: C
options.text: Normalise the strings first, then drop the duplicates, then count

options.label: D
options.text: Any order gives the same result, because the three steps are independent of each other

questions.explanation: Both dropping duplicates and counting rest on comparing strings character by character, so they are only correct once the variants of one city have been folded into a single form - which is why normalising has to come first. Drop the duplicates first and " Ha Noi" and "ha noi" from the same email still count as two different records, so the duplicate survives the cleanup. Count first and one city is torn into three groups, and that number has not removed the duplicates either, so it is of no use for anything. This is exactly why the order of cleaning steps cannot be shuffled at will.

lessons.title: New columns from whole-column arithmetic
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 32: New columns from whole-column arithmetic

theory.contentHtml:
The orders table has a qty column and a price column. Accounting needs to know how much money each row brings in, which means adding a revenue column:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "product": ["Keyboard", "Mouse", "Monitor"],
    "qty": [2, 5, 1],
    "price": [350000, 120000, 2800000],
})
orders["revenue"] = orders["qty"] * orders["price"]
print(orders)
    product  qty    price  revenue
0  Keyboard    2   350000   700000
1     Mouse    5   120000   600000
2   Monitor    1  2800000  2800000

The right-hand side multiplies two columns, and pandas reads that as "multiply each pair of values at the same position", not as multiplying two numbers. The result is a Series exactly as long as the table has rows, and the assignment then attaches that Series to the table under the name you wrote in the square brackets.

A for loop over the rows gives the same answer, but it is longer and noticeably slower: the loop runs in Python, one row per turn, while whole-column multiplication runs in the C layer under pandas over the entire array in a single pass.

A new column lands at the end of the table

Assigning to a name that does not exist yet appends that column at the end of the table. Assigning to a name that already exists overwrites it, with no confirmation and no warning - so a typo in a column name costs you the old data. Column order is therefore the order in which you created them; to slip a column into the middle you have to say where explicitly with orders.insert(1, "sku", ...).

A column you just created is usable on the very next line:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "product": ["Keyboard", "Mouse"],
    "qty": [2, 5],
    "price": [350000, 120000],
})
orders["revenue"] = orders["qty"] * orders["price"]
orders["revenue_k"] = (orders["revenue"] / 1000).round(1)
print(orders)
    product  qty   price  revenue  revenue_k
0  Keyboard    2  350000   700000      700.0
1     Mouse    5  120000   600000      600.0

A single value fills the whole column

orders["channel"] = "web" writes that one string into every row, so you do not have to repeat it three times. When the right-hand side is a list, though, its length has to match the number of rows: off by one element and pandas raises ValueError on the spot instead of truncating or padding for you.

A single value fills the whole column

lessons.rawTitle: Bài 34: Turning codes into labels with map and replace

theory.contentHtml:
The status column in the orders table holds one-letter codes: P, S, C. Whoever reads the report does not know that code table by heart, so they need a readable label column. The job is looking each value up in a dictionary, and map does exactly that:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    "status": ["P", "S", "C", "X"],
})
labels = {"P": "Pending", "S": "Shipped", "C": "Cancelled"}
orders["status_label"] = orders["status"].map(labels)
print(orders)
   order_id status status_label
0         1      P      Pending
1         2      S      Shipped
2         3      C    Cancelled
3         4      X          NaN

An unknown code becomes a missing cell, and nobody tells you

Order 4 carries the code X, which is not in labels. map neither keeps the old value nor raises an error: it writes NaN, a missing cell. The program carries on as normal, the label column still looks fine, and a handful of empty rows simply sit among the other few thousand.

Real data is full of unknown codes: the source system adds a new status, someone types lowercase, or a stray space sneaks in. So after map, look at which cells came out empty and then decide what belongs in them:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    "status": ["P", "S", "C", "X"],
})
labels = {"P": "Pending", "S": "Shipped", "C": "Cancelled"}
orders["status_label"] = orders["status"].map(labels)
print(orders.loc[orders["status_label"].isna(), "status"].tolist())
orders["status_label"] = orders["status_label"].fillna("Unknown")
print(orders)
['X']
   order_id status status_label
0         1      P      Pending
1         2      S      Shipped
2         3      C    Cancelled
3         4      X      Unknown

replace patches a few values and leaves the rest alone

When you do not want to translate a whole column but only fix a few values written off-standard, replace fits better: anything missing from the dictionary is left as it is.

import pandas as pd

customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "name": ["An", "Binh", "Chi"],
    "city": ["HN", "hanoi", "Da Nang"],
})
customers["city"] = customers["city"].replace({"HN": "Ha Noi", "hanoi": "Ha Noi"})
print(customers)
   name     city
0    An   Ha Noi
1  Binh   Ha Noi
2   Chi  Da Nang

Choosing between them is choosing how unknown values are treated: map calls everything outside the dictionary missing data, replace calls it valid and does not touch it.

lessons.title: apply when the rule needs a whole row
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 36: apply when the rule needs a whole row

theory.contentHtml:
The company shipping policy: an order in Ha Noi worth 500,000 or more ships free, everything else costs 30,000. The rule looks at two columns at once, and apply lets you write it almost the way people say it out loud:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi"],
    "revenue": [600000, 400000, 200000],
})


def ship_fee(row):
    if row["city"] == "Ha Noi" and row["revenue"] >= 500000:
        return 0
    return 30000


orders["ship_fee"] = orders.apply(ship_fee, axis=1)
print(orders)
      city  revenue  ship_fee
0   Ha Noi   600000         0
1  Da Nang   400000     30000
2   Ha Noi   200000     30000

axis=1 is the part that matters most: it tells pandas to walk along rows, so on each call the function receives one row as a Series and you pull values out by column name. Drop axis=1 and the default axis=0 takes over, so the function receives each column instead - row["city"] then looks up an index label that does not exist and the program dies. When you only need to transform a single column, call apply on that column directly (orders["revenue"].apply(f)) and the function receives one cell at a time.

Why apply should be the last resort

Underneath, apply is still a Python loop: one function call per row, and each call builds a temporary Series for that row. Whole-column arithmetic makes a single pass in the C layer, so on a table of a few hundred thousand rows the gap is usually tens of times.

The second cost is harder to see: whoever reads the code has to jump into the function body to learn which columns the rule touches. That same shipping rule written with a mask and .loc is both faster and shows the condition right there on the page:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi"],
    "revenue": [600000, 400000, 200000],
})
orders["ship_fee"] = 30000
orders.loc[(orders["city"] == "Ha Noi") & (orders["revenue"] >= 500000), "ship_fee"] = 0
print(orders)
      city  revenue  ship_fee
0   Ha Noi   600000         0
1  Da Nang   400000     30000
2   Ha Noi   200000     30000

So when should you reach for apply? When the rule really is tangled: nested branches, a lookup in an outside table, a library that only accepts one value at a time - to the point where the mask version would be longer and harder to check. In that case give the rule a named function such as ship_fee rather than stuffing a long lambda into the middle of a line, so the next person can still read what the rule says.

lessons.title: Classifying by threshold np.where and cut
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 38: Classifying by threshold np.where and cut

theory.contentHtml:
A grade table needs a result column: 6.5 and above passes, below that fails. There are only two branches and the condition is a True/False mask, so np.where settles it in one line:

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

students = pd.DataFrame({
    "student": ["An", "Binh", "Chi"],
    "score": [8.5, 5.0, 6.5],
})
students["result"] = np.where(students["score"] >= 6.5, "Pass", "Fail")
print(students)
  student  score result
0      An    8.5   Pass
1    Binh    5.0   Fail
2     Chi    6.5   Pass

np.where takes exactly three things: the mask, the value for True rows, the value for False rows. It runs over the whole column in one pass so it is fast, and that is also why it can only choose between two results. Three levels or more means nesting np.where inside np.where, and by the fourth nobody can read it any more.

Several ranges: cut them with cut

pd.cut slices a numeric column into consecutive ranges and labels each one. You pass bins, the list of edges, and labels, the names of the ranges - n ranges need n+1 edges:

import pandas as pd

customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer": ["A", "B", "C", "D"],
    "spend": [0, 1000, 5000, 12000],
})
customers["tier"] = pd.cut(
    customers["spend"],
    bins=[0, 1000, 10000, 100000],
    labels=["Low", "Mid", "High"],
)
print(customers)
  customer  spend  tier
0        A      0   NaN
1        B   1000   Low
2        C   5000   Mid
3        D  12000  High

By default the ranges close on the right

Customer B spent exactly 1000 and lands in Low, not Mid: by default every range is open on the left and closed on the right, that is (0, 1000] and then (1000, 10000]. The second consequence shows up at customer A: 0 is the outermost left edge, so it sits outside every range and becomes a missing cell - the data is still there in spend, it just has no label.

Set right=False and every range flips to closed on the left, open on the right:

import pandas as pd

customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer": ["A", "B", "C", "D"],
    "spend": [0, 1000, 5000, 12000],
})
customers["tier"] = pd.cut(
    customers["spend"],
    bins=[0, 1000, 10000, 100000],
    labels=["Low", "Mid", "High"],
    right=False,
)
print(customers)
  customer  spend  tier
0        A      0   Low
1        B   1000   Mid
2        C   5000   Mid
3        D  12000  High

Picking a side is translating the wording of the task correctly: "1000 and up is Mid" means right=False, while "up to 1000 is still Low" means the default. Read this part carefully, because getting one edge wrong only moves a few customers between groups and raises no error at all.

lessons.title: assign chaining several transformation steps
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 39: assign chaining several transformation steps

theory.contentHtml:
A report usually needs a few steps back to back: compute revenue, convert it to millions, then sort. Written as separate assignments, every step has to repeat the table name, and you either overwrite the original table or spawn a trail of intermediate names like df2, df3. assign folds that sequence into a single chain:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "product": ["Keyboard", "Mouse", "Monitor"],
    "qty": [2, 5, 1],
    "price": [350000, 120000, 2800000],
})
report = (
    orders
    .assign(revenue=lambda d: d["qty"] * d["price"])
    .assign(revenue_m=lambda d: (d["revenue"] / 1000000).round(2))
    .sort_values("revenue", ascending=False)
)
print(report)
print(orders.columns.tolist())
    product  qty    price  revenue  revenue_m
2   Monitor    1  2800000  2800000        2.8
0  Keyboard    2   350000   700000        0.7
1     Mouse    5   120000   600000        0.6
['product', 'qty', 'price']

The last line shows the essential difference: orders still has only its three original columns. assign does not edit the original table; it returns a new one with the column already attached, so you can chain one step onto the next without anything overwriting the starting data.

The lambda receives the table at that step

The right-hand side is written lambda d: ... rather than orders["qty"] * orders["price"], because d is the table at the current step of the chain. That is how the second step can use the revenue column the first step just created - something that never existed in orders. If there is a filter in the middle of the chain, d is the filtered table too, while the name orders still points at the full table and would hand back a longer Series that no longer lines up.

The two columns above also fit into a single call, assign(revenue=..., revenue_m=...): the arguments are evaluated one after another in the order you typed them, so a later column still sees an earlier one.

When a plain assignment is still better

For exactly one new column, df["revenue"] = df["qty"] * df["price"] is shorter and needs no lambda - do not make the reader pay in syntax for a single step. assign also builds a new table at every link, so on very large tables a long chain costs extra memory. And a column name containing a space or a hyphen cannot serve as an argument name, which sends you back to the square brackets.
