lessons.title: Quiz New columns and transformations
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 41: Quiz New columns and transformations

questions.prompt: The table df has 3 rows. What does df["revenue"] = df["qty"] * df["price"] do?

options.label: A
options.text: Multiplies the sum of qty by the sum of price and writes that single number into all three rows

options.label: B
options.text: Only works if you wrap it in a for loop that walks over each row

options.label: C
options.text: Multiplies each pair of values at the same position, then attaches the resulting Series as a new column at the end of the table

options.label: D
options.text: Builds a new table that has a revenue column and leaves the original df untouched

questions.explanation: pandas reads multiplication between two columns position by position: first row with first row, second with second, producing a Series exactly as long as the table has rows. Because the arithmetic already runs over the whole column, a for loop is redundant - which is also why this form is so much faster. It does not collapse the columns into one number; that would need .sum() first. And the assignment writes straight into df: the table gets its new column at the end immediately, unlike assign, which hands back a different table.

questions.prompt: s.map({"P": "Pending", "S": "Shipped"}) meets a value "X" that is not in the dict. What does the matching cell get?

options.label: A
options.text: NaN - a missing cell, and the program carries on as normal

options.label: B
options.text: It keeps "X", since a value that cannot be looked up is left untouched

options.label: C
options.text: The program stops with a KeyError so you know the dict is still missing a code

options.label: D
options.text: An empty string, so the result column stays all text with no missing cells mixed in

questions.explanation: map treats the dict as a complete lookup table: nothing found means no label, so it writes NaN and moves on - no error, no warning, just a few empty cells sitting among the other rows. To keep the old value you need replace, which only touches values that are in the dict. To get a word instead of an empty cell, append .fillna("Unknown") yourself; pandas will not pick a default on your behalf.

questions.prompt: In df.apply(f, axis=1), what does the function f receive on each call?

options.label: A
options.text: One cell at a time, left to right and then down to the next row

options.label: B
options.text: The whole df exactly once, with the function deciding how to walk it

options.label: C
options.text: A tuple of the row's values, accessed by position 0, 1, 2 in column order

options.label: D
options.text: One row as a Series, with values taken by column name such as row["city"]

questions.explanation: axis=1 means walking along rows, so every call receives one row packed into a Series whose index is the column names - which is why row["city"] works. Drop axis=1 and the default axis=0 applies, so the function receives each column rather than the whole table. To receive one cell at a time, call apply on a single column (df["price"].apply(f)) instead of on the DataFrame.

questions.prompt: What is the essential difference between np.where and pd.cut?

options.label: A
options.text: np.where only works on numeric columns while pd.cut only works on text columns

options.label: B
options.text: np.where picks between exactly two results based on one condition, while pd.cut slices a numeric column into consecutive ranges and labels them

options.label: C
options.text: np.where edits the original table in place, while pd.cut always returns a new table

options.label: D
options.text: np.where works out sensible thresholds on its own, while pd.cut makes you declare every edge

questions.explanation: np.where takes a mask plus two values and picks one of them for each row, so it runs out of room as soon as a task has three levels - nesting several layers still runs, but nobody can read it. pd.cut exists for exactly that job: you declare the list of edges and the labels, and it drops each value into its own range. Both of them return a Series rather than writing into the table, so you have to assign to get a column. The condition given to np.where can compare text columns too, whereas pd.cut is the other way round: it needs a numeric column to have ranges to cut at all.

questions.prompt: pd.cut(s, bins=[0, 10, 20], labels=["A", "B"]) where s holds the two values 10 and 0. What labels do those two values get?

options.label: A
options.text: 10 gets B and 0 gets A - each value belongs to the range that starts at it

options.label: B
options.text: Both get A, since 0 and 10 are both edges of the first range

options.label: C
options.text: 10 gets A, and 0 becomes a missing cell because it falls outside every range

options.label: D
options.text: The program raises an error, because a value landing exactly on an edge is undefined

questions.explanation: By default pd.cut builds ranges that are open on the left and closed on the right: (0, 10] labelled A and (10, 20] labelled B. The value 10 therefore closes the first range and gets A. The value 0 is the outermost left edge, and that edge is open, so it belongs to no range and gets NaN - the data is still in the original column, it simply has no label, and nothing is raised. If you want 0 in the first group and 10 in the second, pass right=False to flip which side every range closes on.

questions.prompt: After report = df.assign(revenue=lambda d: d["qty"] * d["price"]), what does df look like?

options.label: A
options.text: df has gained a revenue column, and report is just another name pointing at it

options.label: B
options.text: df keeps its old columns; the revenue column exists only in report

options.label: C
options.text: Both df and report have a revenue column, because assign edits in place and also returns the table

options.label: D
options.text: The program raises an error: to keep the result, assign has to be given inplace=True

questions.explanation: assign builds a new table with the column already attached and returns it, without touching the original - that is exactly what lets you chain several transformation steps without any of them overwriting the starting data. To give df the new column, assign back (df = df.assign(...)) or write df["revenue"] = ... directly. assign also has no inplace parameter, and that is a design decision rather than an oversight: a function that edits in place cannot stand in the middle of a chain.

lessons.title: Grouping rows with groupby
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 42: Grouping rows with groupby

theory.contentHtml:
The orders table keeps one row per order. Your manager asks which city sells best, and the answer isn't in any single row - it only appears once the orders from the same city are added together:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho", "Da Nang"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70],
})
print(orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum())
city
Can Tho     50
Da Nang    150
Ha Noi     320
Name: revenue, dtype: int64

pandas does this in three beats: split the table into groups by the value of the city column, apply the sum to the revenue column inside each group, then combine the numbers back into one result. You write groupby("city") for the first beat and .sum() for the middle one; pandas takes care of the last.

The group key becomes the index

The result is a Series, and the left-hand side isn't 0, 1, 2 but the names of the three cities. The group key has turned into the index instead of staying a column. The three cities also come out in A→Z order because groupby sorts group keys by default, so the result is stable no matter how jumbled the input table was.

That gets in the way at the very next step: an index can't be used like a column. Writing total["city"] raises an error, and if you want to sort by city name or join this result with another table, you need city to be a proper column.

reset_index() turns the key back into a column

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho", "Da Nang"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70],
})
total = orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum().reset_index()
print(total)
      city  revenue
0  Can Tho       50
1  Da Nang      150
2   Ha Noi      320

Now the result is a two-column DataFrame, the index is renumbered 0, 1, 2, and total["city"] works. Filtering, sorting on several columns, exporting to CSV - everything downstream is easier once the group key sits in a column. Note that the revenue column still carries its old name revenue even though the values are totals now; if you want the name to match the content, change it with rename(columns={"revenue": "total_revenue"}).

The missing-key trap

By default groupby uses dropna=True: a row with NaN in the group key forms no group and disappears from the report. This is especially dangerous for money because grouped totals can be smaller than the whole-table total without an error. If "unknown city" is still a business group you must retain, use groupby("city", dropna=False); if exclusion is intentional, count and report the dropped rows first.

lessons.title: Several metrics in one pass with agg
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 44: Several metrics in one pass with agg

theory.contentHtml:
The weekly report needs three numbers per city: total revenue, average revenue per order, and the order count. Calling groupby three times and stitching the three results together is long-winded, while agg accepts a whole list of operations directly:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70, 100],
})
print(orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].agg(["sum", "mean", "count"]).round(1))
         sum   mean  count
city                      
Can Tho   50   50.0      1
Da Nang  150   75.0      2
Ha Noi   420  140.0      3

This time the result is a DataFrame: one row per city, one column per operation. Except the column names are sum, mean, count - the names of the operations, not business names. Hand this table to someone else and they have to guess what count is counting.

Naming the columns while you aggregate

The column_name=(source_column, function) form lets you declare both the source and the target name on a single line:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70, 100],
})
report = orders.groupby("city").agg(
    total_revenue=("revenue", "sum"),
    order_count=("revenue", "count"),
    avg_revenue=("revenue", "mean"),
).reset_index()
report["avg_revenue"] = report["avg_revenue"].round(1)
print(report)
      city  total_revenue  order_count  avg_revenue
0  Can Tho             50            1         50.0
1  Da Nang            150            2         75.0
2   Ha Noi            420            3        140.0

The second benefit shows up when the table has several numeric columns. Write orders.groupby("city").agg(["sum", "count"]) and pandas applies both operations to every numeric column, returning a table with two-level column names like ("revenue", "sum") - hard to read, and harder to pull values out of, since you have to write report[("revenue", "sum")]. The naming form above gives flat, single-level column names you use like any ordinary column.

lessons.title: Grouping on several keys
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 46: Grouping on several keys

theory.contentHtml:
Revenue by city is done. Your manager's next question: inside each city, does online or in-store bring in more? That one needs grouping on two columns at once, and groupby accepts a list directly:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang"],
    "channel": ["online", "store", "online", "online", "store"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70],
})
print(orders.groupby(["city", "channel"])["revenue"].sum())
city     channel
Da Nang  online     200
         store       70
Ha Noi   online     170
         store       80
Name: revenue, dtype: int64

Every row is now a city–channel pair, and pandas aggregates every pair that appears in the data. The empty city cell on the second row does not mean data is missing: that row still belongs to Da Nang, pandas simply drops the repeated label to keep the output readable.

A multi-level index gets in the way

The index of this Series has two levels: city on the outer one, channel on the inner one. Assign the result to total and pulling out a single value means writing the whole key pair, total[("Ha Noi", "store")]; sorting by revenue means working out where revenue sits relative to the two key levels; filtering just the pairs above 100 is more roundabout still.

Which is why reset_index() is almost always the next step

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang"],
    "channel": ["online", "store", "online", "online", "store"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70],
})
totals = orders.groupby(["city", "channel"])["revenue"].sum().reset_index()
print(totals)
      city channel  revenue
0  Da Nang  online      200
1  Da Nang   store       70
2   Ha Noi  online      170
3   Ha Noi   store       80

A single reset_index() pushes both key levels out into ordinary columns, without you naming a level. From here the table is as flat as any other: totals[totals["revenue"] > 100] filters, sort_values sorts, totals["city"] fetches. This long form - one row per key pair plus one value - is also exactly the shape the next lesson will rotate into a grid.

lessons.title: Attaching a group-wide number to every row
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 48: Attaching a group-wide number to every row

theory.contentHtml:
The table holds five orders. You want to add a column showing what percentage of its city's revenue each order accounts for. The number you divide by is the total of the whole group, but the result has to sit on every row - and groupby with sum shortens the table instead:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho", "Da Nang"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70],
})
print(orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum())
print("rows in:", len(orders))
city
Can Tho     50
Da Nang    150
Ha Noi     320
Name: revenue, dtype: int64
rows in: 5

Five rows in, three rows out. That is what agg is: each group collapses into a single value. This result cannot be attached back to the original table, because there is no way to lay three numbers over five rows without saying which row takes which number.

transform returns exactly as many rows as the original table

transform also computes per group, but instead of returning one value per group it hands that value back out to every row belonging to the group:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Can Tho", "Da Nang"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70],
})
city_total = orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].transform("sum")
result = orders.assign(share_pct=(orders["revenue"] / city_total * 100).round(1))
print(result)
      city  revenue  share_pct
0   Ha Noi      120       37.5
1  Da Nang       80       53.3
2   Ha Noi      200       62.5
3  Can Tho       50      100.0
4  Da Nang       70       46.7

city_total is a five-element Series sharing the index of the original table: both Ha Noi rows receive 320, both Da Nang rows receive 150. Because the index matches, dividing straight away with orders["revenue"] / city_total lets pandas pair row with row, with no aligning on your part.

Which one to reach for

Questions shaped like "how much per group" call for agg, and the answer is a summary table shorter than the original. Questions shaped like "where does this row stand against its group" call for transform, and the answer is exactly as long as the original table and attaches straight onto it. Share of total, distance from the group mean, rank within the group all belong to the second kind.

lessons.title: Cross tables with pivot_table and crosstab
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 50: Cross tables with pivot_table and crosstab

theory.contentHtml:
The revenue table for city–channel pairs is tiring to read in long form: to find out whether Ha Noi sells more online or in store, your eye has to hunt down two rows and compare them. Lay the same data out as a grid and the comparison takes a second:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho"],
    "channel": ["online", "store", "online", "online", "store", "store"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70, 40],
})
print(orders.pivot_table(index="city", columns="channel", values="revenue",
                         aggfunc="sum", fill_value=0))
channel  online  store
city                  
Can Tho       0     40
Da Nang     200     70
Ha Noi      170     80

The first four arguments split four roles between them: index is what runs down the rows, columns is what spreads across as columns, values is the numeric column poured into the cells, aggfunc is how to combine when one cell covers several orders. Ha Noi sold online twice, so that cell reads 170.

fill_value=0 handles the rest. Can Tho has no online order, and without this argument that cell would be NaN - dragging the whole online column into floats, printing 200.0 with NaN mixed in. For revenue, "no orders" genuinely means 0, so filling with 0 is reasonable; but for data like exam scores or temperatures NaN is the honest answer, so don't fill with 0 out of reflex.

crosstab when all you need is a count

If the question is "how many orders does each city have per channel", there is no value column to combine at all, only rows to count. crosstab exists for exactly that:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho"],
    "channel": ["online", "store", "online", "online", "store", "store"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 200, 50, 70, 40],
})
print(pd.crosstab(orders["city"], orders["channel"]))
channel  online  store
city                  
Can Tho       0      1
Da Nang       1      1
Ha Noi        2      1

It takes two Series directly rather than column names, and empty cells are already 0 by default.

Grid or long form

The grid wins when you are reading with your eyes and the horizontal axis has only a few values - two channels, four quarters, seven days of the week. The long form from groupby wins when there is more processing to come, because every column is still a real column to filter and sort on, and once the horizontal axis has dozens of values the grid spreads wider than any screen can hold.

Grid or long form

lessons.title: Quiz Grouping and aggregation
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 52: Quiz Grouping and aggregation

questions.prompt: What does orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum() return?

options.label: A
options.text: A two-column DataFrame of city and revenue, with the index renumbered from 0

options.label: B
options.text: A Series indexed by city name, one total value per city

options.label: C
options.text: The original table with its row count intact, plus a column holding the city total

options.label: D
options.text: A single number, the total revenue of the entire table

questions.explanation: Picking out one column and then aggregating gives a Series: one value per group, with the group key sitting in the index rather than in a column. To get a two-column DataFrame indexed 0, 1, 2 you have to chain .reset_index() - that is a later step, not what sum() hands back. Keeping the row count and attaching the group total to each row is the job of transform, while a single number is what you get from orders["revenue"].sum() with no grouping at all.

questions.prompt: After total = orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum(), why do people almost always add .reset_index()?

options.label: A
options.text: Because the groups come out jumbled and reset_index() reorders them A→Z

options.label: B
options.text: Because without it the result has not been computed yet; sum() only describes the work to do

options.label: C
options.text: Because reset_index() merges rows sharing a key, so no group is counted twice

options.label: D
options.text: Because the city names are in the index; moving them into a column is what lets you filter, sort and rename them like any ordinary column

questions.explanation: An index cannot be used as a column: total["city"] raises an error, and every familiar operation - sort_values on two criteria, filtering by city name - needs city to be a real column. reset_index() does exactly that one thing, and it never touches the values. The A→Z order is already there because groupby sorts group keys by default. As for merging rows that share a key, groupby itself already did that; after that step no duplicate key is left to merge.

questions.prompt: You need one row per city with two columns already named total_revenue and order_count. Which call produces exactly that?

options.label: A
options.text: orders.groupby("city").agg(["sum", "count"])

options.label: B
options.text: orders.groupby("city").sum(["total_revenue", "order_count"])

options.label: C
options.text: orders.groupby("city").agg(total_revenue=("revenue", "sum"), order_count=("revenue", "count"))

options.label: D
options.text: orders.groupby("city")[["total_revenue", "order_count"]].agg("sum")

questions.explanation: The target_name=(source_column, function) form declares both the source and the name on one line, so the resulting table carries flat column names exactly as wanted. Passing a list of operations names the columns sum and count - the names of the operations rather than business names - and if the table has several numeric columns the names even become two-level, like ("revenue", "sum"). The two remaining options both mention total_revenue and order_count as though they already existed in the input table, when those are precisely the columns you are trying to create.

questions.prompt: You print orders.groupby(["city", "channel"])["revenue"].sum() and the second row has an empty city cell. What does that mean?

options.label: A
options.text: That row still belongs to the city written on the line above; pandas just drops the repeated label to keep the output readable

options.label: B
options.text: Those are orders whose city could not be determined, which pandas gathers into a group of their own

options.label: C
options.text: The empty cell is a missing value and has to be filled with fillna before you compute anything else

options.label: D
options.text: The result is broken, because grouping on two keys requires calling reset_index() immediately

questions.explanation: Grouping on two keys gives a two-level index, and when printing it pandas writes the outer label only on the first line of each block so the table stays readable - the data underneath is complete, and calling .reset_index() shows the city name repeated on every row. So there is no missing value here for fillna to fix, and no group of anonymous orders either. reset_index() is only a convenience for whatever comes next; skip it and the result is still correct.

questions.prompt: You want to add a column showing what share of its city's revenue each order accounts for. Which approach is right?

options.label: A
options.text: Count the orders per city with count() and multiply by each row's revenue

options.label: B
options.text: Divide orders["revenue"] straight by orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum()

options.label: C
options.text: Call orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum() and assign the result to a new column of the table

options.label: D
options.text: Divide orders["revenue"] by orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].transform("sum")

questions.explanation: transform returns a Series exactly as long as the original table and sharing its index, each row carrying the total of its own group, so dividing the revenue column straight by it lets pandas pair row with row. Both options built on sum() trip over the same thing: the result has one row per city and its index is the city name, which does not align with the index of the original table - divide and you get NaN everywhere, assign it to a new column and the same happens. And counting orders then multiplying produces no share at all; dividing by the group total is what is needed.

questions.prompt: pivot_table(index="city", columns="channel", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum") with no fill_value. What lands in the cell of a city–channel pair with no orders?

options.label: A
options.text: 0, because the sum of an empty set is always 0

options.label: B
options.text: NaN, and the whole column holding it turns to floats; pass fill_value=0 if you want 0

options.label: C
options.text: The pair is dropped from the table, so the grid has fewer columns than there are actual channels

options.label: D
options.text: The program stops with an error; pivot_table demands at least one row for every pair

questions.explanation: A grid always holds every pair of row label and column label, including pairs with no data row behind them, and that empty cell is filled with NaN. Because NaN is a float, the whole column follows it into floats and the table prints 200.0 instead of 200 - enough to make a character-by-character comparison fail. Passing fill_value=0 puts 0 into exactly those cells. No error is raised, and the column stays in the table rather than disappearing.

lessons.title: Joining two tables on a shared key column
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 53: Joining two tables on a shared key column

theory.contentHtml:
The orders table only records customer_id, while customer names live in the contacts table. Your manager wants an orders table where the buyer's name is readable right away. The job is to bring the two tables together through the column they both have:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103],
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 1],
    "amount": [240000, 150000, 600000],
})
customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 3],
    "name": ["An", "Binh", "Chi"],
})
print(orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id"))
   order_id  customer_id  amount  name
0       101            1  240000    An
1       102            2  150000  Binh
2       103            1  600000    An

on="customer_id" says the two tables meet through that column, so it has to exist on both sides (if the names differ, use left_on and right_on). For each order row, pandas finds the customer row carrying that key value and pastes the remaining columns into the same line. Orders 101 and 103 both belong to customer 1, so both pick up the name An - one row on the right can serve many rows on the left. The result is a new table, the two original tables are untouched, and the row labels are renumbered from 0.

Default: rows whose key does not match are dropped

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103],
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 9],
    "amount": [240000, 150000, 600000],
})
customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 3],
    "name": ["An", "Binh", "Chi"],
})
joined = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id")
print(joined)
print(len(orders), len(joined))
   order_id  customer_id  amount  name
0       101            1  240000    An
1       102            2  150000  Binh
3 2

The orders table has three rows, the result has two. Order 103 belongs to customer 9 and nobody in the contacts table carries that number, so it falls out of the result; customer 3, who has never ordered anything, does not show up either. This is an inner join, what merge does when you say nothing else: keep only the key values present on both sides. Losing rows this way comes with no warning at all, so counting the rows again after a join is a habit worth keeping.

Missing keys differ from SQL

pandas has one important difference: two NaN keys can match during merge, while NULL = NULL is not TRUE in SQL. If a missing key means "customer unknown", joining two missing values is a business error. Count them with orders["customer_id"].isna().sum(), then drop, fill or separate them before merging according to the data contract.

lessons.title: Four join types inner, left, right, outer
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 55: Four join types inner, left, right, outer

theory.contentHtml:
In the previous lesson, order 103 vanished from the result just because its customer code was missing from the contacts table. That order is real money, and a revenue report that leaves it out is a wrong report. The how parameter decides which side keeps all of its rows:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103],
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 9],
    "amount": [240000, 150000, 600000],
})
customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 3],
    "name": ["An", "Binh", "Chi"],
})
print(orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left"))
print(orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="right"))
   order_id  customer_id  amount  name
0       101            1  240000    An
1       102            2  150000  Binh
2       103            9  600000   NaN
   order_id  customer_id    amount  name
0     101.0            1  240000.0    An
1     102.0            2  150000.0  Binh
2       NaN            3       NaN   Chi

how="left" keeps every row of the table written on the left of the call - the orders here - and fills NaN into the columns taken from the right when no matching row is found. Order 103 is still there, we simply do not know the customer name yet. how="right" does the opposite: every customer shows up, customer 3 who has bought nothing gets an empty order_id and amount, and order 103 is the one that falls out.

Notice that the order_id column in the second table prints 101.0. An integer column that gains an empty cell makes pandas convert the whole column to floats, because NaN is not an integer - the price of keeping the unmatched rows.

outer keeps both sides

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103],
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 9],
    "amount": [240000, 150000, 600000],
})
customers = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 3],
    "name": ["An", "Binh", "Chi"],
})
print(orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="outer"))
   order_id  customer_id    amount  name
0     101.0            1  240000.0    An
1     102.0            2  150000.0  Binh
2       NaN            3       NaN   Chi
3     103.0            9  600000.0   NaN

No row is dropped, and outer sorts the result by ascending key value instead of keeping the order of the left-hand table.

Why left is the usual pick

Most of the time when you join tables, you have an event table that must stay intact (orders, transactions) and a lookup table that enriches it (customer names, product categories). Losing an event row means wrong figures, whereas a lookup table missing a few odd codes only leaves empty cells that you can see and deal with. how="left" describes that balance exactly, while inner quietly deletes the evidence.

headings.text: outer keeps both sides
Why left is the usual pick

theory.contentHtml:
The revenue report ran correctly for three months straight. Then somebody joined the contacts table in to show customer emails, touched nothing about the money column, and total revenue doubled:

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({
    "order_id": [101, 102, 103],
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 3],
    "amount": [100000, 200000, 300000],
})
contacts = pd.DataFrame({
    "customer_id": [1, 2, 3, 3, 3],
    "email": ["an@shop.vn", "binh@shop.vn", "chi@shop.vn", "chi@work.vn", "chi@old.vn"],
})
joined = orders.merge(contacts, on="customer_id")
print(joined)
print(orders["amount"].sum(), joined["amount"].sum())
print(orders.shape, joined.shape)
   order_id  customer_id  amount         email
0       101            1  100000    an@shop.vn
1       102            2  200000  binh@shop.vn
2       103            3  300000   chi@shop.vn
3       103            3  300000   chi@work.vn
4       103            3  300000    chi@old.vn
600000 1200000
(3, 3) (5, 4)

Customer 3 has three rows in the contacts table, so order 103 is multiplied into three rows and 300000 is added three times. Nobody typed the wrong amount, nobody changed the total formula, the number still comes out and still looks ordinary. The cause is always the same: the key is duplicated in the other table.

The cheapest warning sign is shape: a join meant to enrich data has to keep the row count, so 3 turning into 5 is already reason enough to stop and check. The weakness of this method is that you have to remember to look.

Two ways to make the machine defend you

import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [101, 102], "customer_id": [1, 9], "amount": [100000, 200000]})
contacts = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [1, 1, 3], "email": ["an@a.vn", "an@b.vn", "chi@a.vn"]})
try:
    orders.merge(contacts, on="customer_id", validate="m:1")
except Exception as err:
    print(type(err).__name__)
print(orders.merge(contacts, on="customer_id", how="outer", indicator=True))
MergeError
   order_id  customer_id    amount     email      _merge
0     101.0            1  100000.0   an@a.vn        both
1     101.0            1  100000.0   an@b.vn        both
2       NaN            3       NaN  chi@a.vn  right_only
3     102.0            9  200000.0       NaN   left_only

validate="m:1" is a declaration about the shape of your data: on the left a key may repeat freely, on the right each key must have exactly one row. pandas checks that declaration before joining, and if it is wrong it raises MergeError right at the merge line instead of letting you discover it three weeks later through a number that is off.

indicator=True adds a _merge column telling you where each row came from: both means it matched, left_only is an order with no customer, right_only is a customer with no order. One outer join with this column shows all three groups at once, including the spot where customer 1 takes up two rows.

lessons.title: Stacking tables by rows and by columns
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 58: Stacking tables by rows and by columns

theory.contentHtml:
Every month the sales team exports a revenue table: same columns, different data. To look at the whole quarter you have to stack them on top of each other. This is not a job for merge - there is no key to look anything up by, it is just appending:

import pandas as pd

jan = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Ha Noi", "Hue"], "revenue": [120, 80]})
feb = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Ha Noi", "Vinh"], "revenue": [150, 60]})
print(pd.concat([jan, feb]))
print(pd.concat([jan, feb], ignore_index=True))
     city  revenue
0  Ha Noi      120
1     Hue       80
0  Ha Noi      150
1    Vinh       60
     city  revenue
0  Ha Noi      120
1     Hue       80
2  Ha Noi      150
3    Vinh       60

pd.concat takes a list of tables and stacks them by rows by default (axis=0). The first table contributes two rows labelled 0 and 1, the second brings along its own labels 0 and 1, so the result has repeated labels. Duplicate labels do not raise an error right away, but they will cause trouble the moment you write .loc[0] and get two rows back. ignore_index=True throws the old labels away and numbers the rows continuously - almost always what you want when combining data of the same kind. The tables are matched by column name, not by column position, and a column present in only one table leaves NaN in the remaining rows.

Stacking by columns

import pandas as pd

revenue = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["Ha Noi", "Hue"], "revenue": [120, 80]})
cost = pd.DataFrame({"cost": [70, 50]})
print(pd.concat([revenue, cost], axis=1))
     city  revenue  cost
0  Ha Noi      120    70
1     Hue       80    50

axis=1 places the tables side by side. Which row pairs with which is decided here by the row labels, not by a key column: the row labelled 0 in one table shares a line with the row labelled 0 in the other. If the two tables have mismatched labels, the result is full of NaN even though the data looks like it should line up.

When to concat, when to merge

Same set of columns, different data, and you want more rows: that is concat. Same set of objects, different information, and you want more columns: that is merge. The easy mistake is joining by columns - if two tables merely happen to have the same number of rows without their rows meaning the same thing, concat(axis=1) will glue one customer's data onto another's without saying a word. Whenever there is a shared identifier column, use merge.

lessons.title: Date columns and grouping by month
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 60: Date columns and grouping by month

theory.contentHtml:
The sales table has a date column read from a file, and as far as pandas is concerned it is still just text like "2026-01-05". Text can be compared alphabetically, but you cannot add or subtract days with it, it does not know which month it belongs to, and you cannot group by month with it. The first step is always converting the type:

import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "date": ["2026-01-05", "2026-01-20", "2026-02-03", "2026-03-11"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 150, 60],
})
sales["date"] = pd.to_datetime(sales["date"])
sales = sales.set_index("date")
print(sales.loc["2026-02":"2026-03"])
print(sales.index.month.tolist())
            revenue
date               
2026-02-03      150
2026-03-11       60
[1, 1, 2, 3]

pd.to_datetime turns the text column into a real date column, and from there .dt or .index.month can finally answer the question "which month". Moving the date column up to be the row index with set_index opens up the neatest way to filter: sales.loc["2026-02":"2026-03"] takes both months whole - you write the date to whatever precision you like and pandas reads it as that range - and like every .loc slice, both ends are included.

Grouping by month and moving averages

import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "date": ["2026-01-05", "2026-01-20", "2026-02-03", "2026-03-11", "2026-04-02", "2026-04-27"],
    "revenue": [120, 80, 150, 60, 200, 40],
})
sales["date"] = pd.to_datetime(sales["date"])
monthly = sales.set_index("date").resample("ME")[["revenue"]].sum()
monthly["ma3"] = monthly["revenue"].rolling(3).mean().round(1)
print(monthly)
            revenue    ma3
date                      
2026-01-31      200    NaN
2026-02-28      150    NaN
2026-03-31       60  136.7
2026-04-30      240  150.0

resample("ME") gathers the rows into time buckets and aggregates them like groupby, but it generates every bucket in the range on its own - a month with no orders still shows up as a row with the value 0, which groupby does not do. "ME" is the month-end bucket, so the row label is the last day of the month; "D" is by day, "W" by week, "YE" by year.

rolling(3).mean() slides a three-row window down the table and takes the average of that window, which is how you flatten out months that jump. The first two months do not have three values yet, so the result is NaN - that is the correct behaviour, not a bug - and round(1) is there to keep the printed numbers from running to a dozen digits.

The example uses dates without times. For API timestamps, make the timezone explicit: parse UTC values with pd.to_datetime(..., utc=True), then call .dt.tz_convert("Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh") before extracting the local date or month. Mixing naive and timezone-aware timestamps either errors or groups events around midnight incorrectly; DST also means a local day is not always exactly 24 hours long.

lessons.title: Quiz Joining tables and time-based data
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 62: Quiz Joining tables and time-based data

questions.prompt: What does orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id") require of the two tables?

options.label: A
options.text: The two tables must have the same number of rows, with row i of one matching row i of the other

options.label: B
options.text: The customers table must be sorted by customer_id in ascending order before the join

options.label: C
options.text: Both tables must have a column named customer_id; if the names differ, use left_on and right_on

options.label: D
options.text: The customer_id column must be the row index of at least one of the two tables

questions.explanation: on takes the name of the key column, and that name has to exist in both tables because pandas looks it up on both sides. Joining is a matter of matching values, not of lining rows up, so the two sides need not have the same number of rows and the order of the lookup table has no effect on the result - pandas finds the matching row however jumbled the table is. The key column does not have to be the row index either; moving it to the index is only necessary when you want to join on the index with left_index/right_index.

questions.prompt: The orders table has 500 orders, the customers table has 80 customers, and not every order finds a customer. To keep all 500 orders in the report, with the customer name where there is one, which how do you use?

options.label: A
options.text: how="left" with orders written on the left - every order is kept, and unmatched orders get NaN in the name column

options.label: B
options.text: how="inner" - the default, which keeps every row of whichever of the two tables is larger

options.label: C
options.text: how="right" with orders written on the left - it keeps every row of the table before the dot

options.label: D
options.text: how="outer" - the only way to keep all 500 orders, every other type drops rows

questions.explanation: how="left" keeps the table written on the left of the call whole and fills NaN into the columns taken from the right when there is no matching row, which is exactly what keeping all the orders needs. inner keeps only keys present on both sides, so an order with an unknown customer code falls out, and it does not favour the larger table in any way. right keeps the right-hand table whole, that is customers, the opposite of what is wanted. outer really does keep all 500 orders, but it drags in the customers who have never bought anything, adding rows to the report that are not orders at all.

questions.prompt: orders has 3 orders, each from a different customer. The contacts table has 3 rows for customer A and 1 row for each of the others. What happens if you join the two tables on the customer code and then sum the amount column?

options.label: A
options.text: The total is unchanged, because merge drops contact rows that repeat the same customer code

options.label: B
options.text: pandas stops with an error because the key on the right is duplicated

options.label: C
options.text: The total is unchanged, but the email column holds all three of customer A's addresses in one cell

options.label: D
options.text: The result has 5 rows and the total is overcounted, because customer A's order is multiplied into 3 rows

questions.explanation: Every row on the left is joined with every row on the right carrying the same key, so an order that meets three contact rows becomes three result rows with the same amount, and the sum counts that amount three times. pandas does not deduplicate on its own and does not stop either - by default it treats a repeated key as perfectly valid, and only checks once you declare validate. It also never crams several values into one cell; every cell is always a single value, and what swells is the number of rows.

questions.prompt: What does validate="m:1" do in merge?

options.label: A
options.text: Automatically drops the rows with a repeated key on the right so the result is not multiplied

options.label: B
options.text: Checks that each key on the right has only one row, and raises MergeError at join time if not

options.label: C
options.text: Checks that every key of the left-hand table finds a matching row in the right-hand table

options.label: D
options.text: Adds a column telling you which table each result row came from

questions.explanation: m:1 is a declaration about the shape of your data: on the left a key may repeat as much as it likes, on the right each key must have exactly one row. pandas checks that declaration before joining and raises MergeError if it is wrong, so you find out right at the merge line instead of through a number that is off some time later. It only checks, it does not fix anything - if you want one row per key you have to clean the right-hand table yourself. Whether the left-hand keys find a match is not validate's business, and the column recording where each row came from is the job of indicator=True.

questions.prompt: You have 12 revenue tables, one per month, all with the columns city and revenue. You need one table covering the whole year. What do you use?

options.label: A
options.text: merge the 12 tables one after another on the city column

options.label: B
options.text: pd.concat with axis=1 so the 12 tables sit side by side

options.label: C
options.text: pd.concat with ignore_index=True, stacking by rows

options.label: D
options.text: resample("ME") on the list of 12 tables

questions.explanation: Twelve tables with the same set of columns, different data, and you need more rows rather than more columns - that is exactly the job of pd.concat stacking by rows, with ignore_index=True so the row labels do not repeat twelve times over. merge on city would cross the months against each other and multiply the rows, since a city appears in all 12 tables. axis=1 places the tables side by side, so you would get back 24 columns with duplicate names. And resample works on a single table with a time index; it does not take a list of tables.

questions.prompt: A table has dates as its row index and spans three months, but February had no orders at all. What does df.resample("ME").sum() produce?

options.label: A
options.text: Three rows, one per month including February with the value 0, labelled with the last day of each month

options.label: B
options.text: Two rows, because a month with no orders forms no group and is therefore skipped

options.label: C
options.text: One row per day that has orders, with the total column being a running sum accumulated from the top of the table

options.label: D
options.text: A single row holding the revenue of all three months added together

questions.explanation: resample gathers the rows into evenly spaced time buckets and aggregates them, and "ME" is the month-end bucket, so three months of data give three rows labelled with the last day of each month. The most memorable difference from groupby sits precisely at February: resample generates every bucket in the range, so an empty month still appears as a row with the value 0 instead of vanishing, and the time series has no gaps - a chart drawn from this table will not skip over February. The result does not stay at day level either; for that you take the "D" bucket. A running accumulated sum is the job of cumsum, and a single number covering all three months is sum() on the whole table.

lessons.title: Tidying a table for the reader
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 63: Tidying a table for the reader

theory.contentHtml:
The revenue-by-city table has just finished computing. It carries an internal code column, a share column running to twelve decimal places, and the cities sit in whatever order they landed in the file. That table is fine to keep computing on, but paste it into an email to your manager and nobody will read it.

import pandas as pd

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "city_code": ["HN", "DN", "CT", "HUE"],
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho", "Hue"],
    "revenue": [12500000, 4300000, 2100000, 5600000],
    "orders": [42, 17, 9, 20],
})
sales["share"] = sales["revenue"] / sales["revenue"].sum() * 100
print(sales)
print()
report = (
    sales.sort_values("revenue", ascending=False)
    .head(3)[["city", "revenue", "share"]]
    .round({"share": 1})
    .rename(columns={"city": "City", "revenue": "Revenue", "share": "Share %"})
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
print(report)
  city_code     city   revenue  orders      share
0        HN   Ha Noi  12500000      42  51.020408
1        DN  Da Nang   4300000      17  17.551020
2        CT  Can Tho   2100000       9   8.571429
3       HUE      Hue   5600000      20  22.857143

      City   Revenue  Share %
0   Ha Noi  12500000     51.0
1      Hue   5600000     22.9
2  Da Nang   4300000     17.6

Five steps, each one dropping something

sort_values decides the order in which the reader meets the information. head(3) cuts off the tail nobody asked about. The list of columns inside the square brackets both picks the columns and reorders them, so city_code - the system's code, not the reader's - falls out.

round takes a dict so that only the column you name gets rounded and the others stay as they are; those twelve decimal places are how the machine stores the number, not how precise it really is. Finally reset_index(drop=True) numbers the rows again from 0, because the old labels 0, 3, 1 only give away that the table has been sorted - they carry no information of their own.

Column names for the machine, column names for people

While you are analysing, column names are written like code: short, lowercase, no spaces, quick to type and hard to get wrong. In a report it is the reader who has to understand them - Share % states the unit, share does not. Keep rename for the last step, once every calculation is done, so the code above it still refers to the columns by their old names.

Two tables, not one

report is a new table and sales is still intact behind it, and that is deliberate. The analysis table still has to answer the next question, and if you round in place there, every calculation afterwards runs on numbers that have already been trimmed. Rounding belongs to the last step, right before the table goes to a reader.

lessons.title: Exporting a table to CSV and Markdown
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 65: Exporting a table to CSV and Markdown

theory.contentHtml:
The report table is finished, and now it has to leave Python: attached to an email, opened in Excel, or pasted into a document. to_csv handles that, and it has one detail that is easy to miss: given no path it does not write a file, it returns a string.

import pandas as pd

report = pd.DataFrame({
    "City": ["Ha Noi", "Hue", "Da Nang"],
    "Revenue": [12500000, 5600000, 4300000],
})
text = report.to_csv(index=False)
print(text)
print(len(text))
City,Revenue
Ha Noi,12500000
Hue,5600000
Da Nang,4300000

57

text is a 57-character string holding the whole table, with the rows separated by newline characters - that is why print shows it across several lines, and the blank line at the end is there because the string already ends with a newline and print adds one more.

index=False drops the row-label column. Leave it out and the file gains an extra unnamed first column holding 0, 1, 2; open that in Excel and there is a spare column sitting there that nobody can explain.

On your own machine, pass a path

report.to_csv("sales-report.csv", index=False)

Given a path, the function writes straight to the file and returns None. The sandbox for this course runs in the browser and has no disk to write to, so here we always leave the path out and print the string to look at it. Even on a real job, printing it first is a good habit: one wrong column gets fixed on the spot, which beats finding it after the file has already been sent.

A table you can paste straight into a document

print(report.to_markdown(index=False))
| City    |   Revenue |
|:--------|----------:|
| Ha Noi  |  12500000 |
| Hue     |   5600000 |
| Da Nang |   4300000 |

to_markdown returns the table already ruled off, so pasting it into a README, into Notion or into the description box of a pull request shows a real table rather than a wall of text. This block has no Run button because to_markdown needs the tabulate package, which the sandbox does not ship - calling it here gets you ImportError: Missing optional dependency 'tabulate'. On your own machine pip install tabulate once and it works from then on, and that error message is also how pandas tells you which package is missing.

lessons.title: Plotting straight from a DataFrame
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 67: Plotting straight from a DataFrame

theory.contentHtml:
The revenue table for four cities is sorted, but a reader has to study it for a moment before noticing that Ha Noi is nearly six times Can Tho. Four bars side by side show it at once. A DataFrame can plot itself; the data does not have to be moved into some other shape first:

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sales = pd.DataFrame({
    "city": ["Ha Noi", "Da Nang", "Can Tho", "Hue"],
    "revenue": [12500000, 4300000, 2100000, 5600000],
})
top = sales.sort_values("revenue", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
print(top)
top.plot(kind="bar", x="city", y="revenue", legend=False)
plt.ylabel("Revenue (VND)")
plt.title("Revenue by city")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
      city   revenue
0   Ha Noi  12500000
1      Hue   5600000
2  Da Nang   4300000
3  Can Tho   2100000

The figure appears right under the output box. kind picks the kind of chart - "bar" for vertical bars, "barh" for horizontal ones, "line" for a line, "hist" for a distribution - while x and y say which column goes on which axis. legend=False because there is only one series, and a legend that repeats the word "revenue" only takes up room. Sorting before you plot is not decoration: the eye reads a bar chart from left to right, so the tallest bar should sit where the eye lands first.

Print the numbers anyway

A chart gives an impression, not a figure. Whoever reads the report will ask "how much was Ha Noi", and nobody can read that number off the height of a bar. So keep a print next to every chart: the table to quote numbers from, the chart to see the proportions.

Drawing by hand when you need more control

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

monthly = pd.DataFrame({
    "month": ["2026-01", "2026-02", "2026-03", "2026-04"],
    "revenue": [8200000, 9100000, 7600000, 10400000],
})
print(monthly)
plt.plot(monthly["month"], monthly["revenue"], marker="o")
plt.ylabel("Revenue (VND)")
plt.title("Revenue by month")
plt.show()
     month   revenue
0  2026-01   8200000
1  2026-02   9100000
2  2026-03   7600000
3  2026-04  10400000

plt.plot takes two Series directly as the horizontal and vertical axes, and marker="o" puts a dot at every month so you can see how many data points there are. This is wordier than .plot, but you decide each piece yourself, which suits the case where several lines have to go on the same figure.

As for savefig, saving the figure to a file does not work here - the sandbox cannot write files, and there is no need to anyway, since the figure is already showing under the output box.

lessons.title: The shape of an analysis
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 68: The shape of an analysis

theory.contentHtml:
Your manager sends over an orders file and asks exactly one question: which city sells best, and what share of the revenue is that? The file has one row entered twice, city names spelled differently in different places, and a few cancelled orders. The six steps below are things you have already learned, scattered through the course, put back in the right order:

import io
import pandas as pd

csv_text = """order_id,city,status,qty,unit_price
101,Ha Noi,done,2,120000
102, da nang ,done,1,250000
103,Ha Noi,cancelled,3,90000
104,Hue,done,5,60000
105,Ha Noi,done,4,120000
105,Ha Noi,done,4,120000
"""
orders = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(csv_text)).drop_duplicates().copy()
orders["city"] = orders["city"].str.strip().str.title()
orders["revenue"] = orders["qty"] * orders["unit_price"]

done = orders[orders["status"] == "done"]
by_city = (
    done.groupby("city", as_index=False)["revenue"].sum()
    .sort_values("revenue", ascending=False)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
print(by_city)
print(round(by_city["revenue"].iloc[0] / by_city["revenue"].sum() * 100, 1))
      city  revenue
0   Ha Noi   720000
1      Hue   300000
2  Da Nang   250000
56.7

One sentence per step

Read: read_csv takes the CSV text through io.StringIO and gives back a table. Drop duplicates: drop_duplicates removes order 105, which was written twice, and the .copy() is there because a column is added to this table immediately afterwards. Normalise: .str.strip().str.title() pulls " da nang " and a properly capitalised spelling onto the same name. New column: each order's revenue is computed for the whole column in one go. Filter: keep the done orders. Group and conclude: total by city, sort descending, then pull out the two numbers that answer the question that was actually asked.

This order cannot be shuffled

Group before dropping duplicates and order 105 is counted twice. Group before normalising the names and " da nang " and "Da Nang" become two different cities, one row each in the report. Filter for done after grouping and the money from the cancelled order is already inside the total, with no way to take it back out.

The reason is not a rule somebody laid down: an aggregation has no way of knowing which rows are trustworthy, it adds up exactly what you hand it. So everything that dirties the numbers has to be cleaned up before groupby runs.

The last step is an answer, not a table

The question was "which city sells best, and what share is that". The by_city table is not the answer yet, it is only the raw material - the last print is what pulls out the 56.7%. An analysis that stops at the table is an analysis that leaves the hard part to the reader.

practice.title: Practice: Three numbers for the end-of-day report
practice.summaryHtml: At the end of each day the system spits out a raw orders table: some rows written twice because submit was pressed twice, city names typed by hand so the capitalisation is mixed and there is stray whitespace, and cancelled orders in among them. The manager needs exactly three pieces of information, printed in a set order, ready to paste into the daily report message.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.html:
Write the function report_orders(orders). The input table has the columns order_id, city, status, qty, unit_price.

Clean the table by three rules, before computing anything:

  1. Drop rows that are exact duplicates of each other, keeping the first occurrence.
  2. Strip the extra whitespace from both ends of the city name, then capitalise the first letter of each word and lowercase the rest.
  3. Count only the orders whose status is "done".

The revenue of an order is the quantity times the unit price. The function returns exactly three values, in this order:

  1. The number of orders counted, an integer.
  2. The total revenue of those orders, an integer.
  3. The revenue-per-city table, two columns named city and revenue, with revenue ordered from highest to lowest. When two cities have equal revenue, the one whose name comes first alphabetically goes above. The row index is renumbered from 0.

The test case receives the three returned values and prints them one by one. The table passed in must be unchanged after the call.

lessons.rawTitle: Bài 70: Quiz Looking back over the course

questions.prompt: The table df is what is left after a filtering step, so its row labels start at 4. You need the first three rows counting down from the top of the table - how do you write that?

options.label: A
options.text: df.loc[:3]

options.label: C
options.text: df.iloc[:3]

questions.explanation: "The first three rows" is a question of position, and counting by position is what .iloc is for - its slices behave like Python list slices, so asking for three rows of a table that only has two is not an error. Both .loc options go looking for labels instead: df.loc[:3] slices up to the label 3, which does not exist in a table starting at 4, while df.loc[[0, 1, 2]] names three labels that are gone and raises. The last option puts a list inside bare square brackets, and bare square brackets with a list is the syntax for picking columns, not rows.

questions.prompt: To set ship_fee to 0 for every row whose city is "Ha Noi", right on df itself, which way is certain to land?

options.label: A
options.text: df.loc[df["city"] == "Ha Noi", "ship_fee"] = 0

options.label: B
options.text: df[df["city"] == "Ha Noi"]["ship_fee"] = 0

options.label: C
options.text: df.copy().loc[df["city"] == "Ha Noi", "ship_fee"] = 0

options.label: D
options.text: hn = df[df["city"] == "Ha Noi"] and then hn["ship_fee"] = 0

questions.explanation: Putting the row condition and the column name into one .loc call is the only way of telling pandas outright that you mean to write into the original table, so it writes there and says nothing. The two options that filter first and assign afterwards - whether written on one line or split through the variable hn - both assign into the sub-table the filter has just returned, which comes with a SettingWithCopyWarning while df stays exactly as it was. The .copy() option is even more decisive: it makes a copy, edits that copy, then throws it away immediately, because nobody keeps the result.

questions.prompt: An orders table has a row entered twice and a city column with mixed capitalisation ("ha noi" alongside "Ha Noi"). You need revenue per city. Which order produces the right numbers?

options.label: A
options.text: Group by city first, then drop the duplicate rows and normalise the names on the result table

options.label: B
options.text: Drop the duplicate rows, group by city, then normalise the names on the result table

options.label: C
options.text: Normalise the names, group by city, then drop the duplicate rows on the result table

options.label: D
options.text: Normalise the names and drop the duplicate rows first, and only then group by city

questions.explanation: A grouping adds up exactly what you hand it; it has no way of knowing which row is a spare record or which spellings are the same city. So both cleaning jobs have to be finished first: drop duplicates after grouping and the money from the spare row is already in the total with no way back out, while normalising the names after grouping means "ha noi" and "Ha Noi" have become two separate rows, so renaming leaves you with two rows sharing a name and carrying two different numbers. Grouping right at the start walks into both mistakes at once.

questions.prompt: You need to add a city_total column to the orders table: every row carries the total revenue of the whole city that order belongs to. The table has to keep the same number of rows.

options.label: A
options.text: orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].sum()

options.label: B
options.text: orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].transform("sum")

options.label: C
options.text: orders.groupby("city")["revenue"].agg("sum")

options.label: D
options.text: orders["revenue"].sum()

questions.explanation: transform is the only one that keeps the shape: it computes the total for each group and then sends that number back out to every row of the group, so the result is exactly as long as the table and can be assigned straight into a new column. sum() and agg("sum") are the same job written two ways - both shrink the table down to one row per city, and assigning that back into the original fails on length. And orders["revenue"].sum() ignores the grouping altogether: it gives one number for the whole table, so every row would carry the same value.

questions.prompt: orders has 100 rows, one order each, with a total_amount column. order_items has 380 line-item rows. After merging the two tables on order_id and then summing total_amount, the number comes out several times larger than reality. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: The merge keeps the rows that do not match by default, and those empty rows add to the total

options.label: B
options.text: The merge turns the numeric column into text, so the sum becomes string concatenation and produces a huge number

options.label: C
options.text: The merge re-sorts the table by the key, so some rows get repeated while the order is being changed

options.label: D
options.text: One order has several line items, so its total_amount is repeated on each of them and gets added several times

questions.explanation: A one-to-many merge gives a result of 380 rows rather than 100, and each line-item row carries a full copy of the order's information - total_amount included. Summing that column adds each order once per line item it has, so the total inflates by exactly that ratio. The default merge is inner, keeping only the rows that match, so no empty rows creep in; the data types of the columns are not changed by the merge either; and the row order does change, but changing the order creates no extra rows. To get the total right, sum on the orders table before merging.

questions.prompt: text = report.to_csv(index=False) - what is text?

options.label: A
options.text: None, because the function has written the table out to a default file named report.csv

options.label: B
options.text: A new DataFrame, the same as the old one but with every column converted to text

options.label: C
options.text: A string holding the whole table in CSV form, with the rows separated by newline characters

options.label: D
options.text: The number of rows written, so you can check whether the table holds all the data

questions.explanation: Given no path, to_csv has nowhere to write, so it returns the entire content as a string - print(text) shows several lines precisely because that string contains newline characters. The function only returns None when you give it a path, and it never invents a filename on your behalf. The result is not a table either: exporting to CSV is the point where the data leaves the DataFrame world. To find out how many rows a table has, use len(), which is a different question.
